data.title: Is Nvidia's Colette Kress Standing On A Glass Cliff?
data.description:
A founder-CEO of an all-important global AI company, with a rockstar persona, admits to an affair with an alleged spy.

He is made to resign with the whole world watching and many powerful people rooting for his return, while waxing eloquent about why he is indispensable and irreplaceable.

A significant section of employees, at least a fourth of the workforce, feel wronged on his behalf, showing where their loyalties lie.

Many Shareholders want him back while the stock is in steady decline

It is in these evidently hostile conditions that a senior woman executive has been brought in to steady the ship while the company looks for a permanent successor.

Nvidia CFO Colette Kress’s appointment as interim chief of a company seen as the linchpin of the global AI boom is among the toughest jobs in the world right now.

It has also reignited the debate around the glass cliff phenomenon.

What is the glass cliff?

The term describes the widespread practice of preferentially appointing women or other minority employees to leadership positions in times of crisis, when the chances of failure are highest.

That makes it even harder for them to perform, eventually reinforcing the perception that women cannot lead.

It was coined by British academics Michelle Ryan and Alex Haslam, who in 2004 published an extensive study of FTSE 100 companies and found that women tended to be appointed to lead failing organisations.

A pattern that runs through history

Examples abound.

Marissa Mayer became Yahoo’s CEO in 2012, when the internet major had lost substantial market share and was struggling with focus and innovation.

She was its fifth CEO in five years, a sign of how volatile the company was.

Ellen Pao at Reddit (RDDT), Roz Brewer at Walgreens Boots (WBA), even Theresa May becoming UK prime minister right after Brexit: all are telltale signs of the insidious phenomenon.

In a study conducted by Alison Cook, professor of management at the Jon M Huntsman School of Business at Utah State University, and her colleague Christy Glass, professor at the university’s school of social sciences, the researchers found that in US college men’s basketball, coaches from racial minorities were more likely than white coaches to be promoted to losing teams.

In 2013, the duo analysed CEO transitions in Fortune 500 companies over 15 years.

They found that occupational minorities, defined as white women and men and women of colour, were more likely than white men to be promoted CEO of weakly performing firms.

They also found that when performance declined under occupational minority CEOs, these leaders were likely to be replaced by white men, a pattern they termed the “savior effect.”

Does Nvidia fit the picture?

Invezz asked Cook whether Kress’s appointment amounts to a glass cliff, given that Nvidia (NVDA) is doing exceptionally well financially and has strong prospects.

“The glass cliff isn’t only about weak performance. It’s about being appointed to a precarious situation,” Cook told Invezz.

“In my work with Dr. Christy Glass, we’ve treated firms facing a scandal, including the firing of the previous CEO, or going through major restructuring as glass cliff situations too. Nvidia fits that picture. Kress is stepping in during a national security investigation, several lawsuits, and a permanent CEO search that may not pick her,” she said.

Cook spells out the challenges Kress faces and the conditions she is leading under, which make this a compelling case of the phenomenon.

“First, the scrutiny will be enormous. Nvidia is one of the most visible companies in the world, and every decision she makes will be watched and second-guessed. Second, her authority may be challenged. She is leading while there is a very public push to bring her predecessor back, which can make it hard for anyone to lead with full support. Third, the reputational risk falls on her."

"She is now the face of the company during a crisis she didn’t create, and if things go badly, she may be the one who wears it. So while the business itself is strong, the circumstances around her appointment fit the glass cliff mould,” she said.

Why organisations turn to women in a crisis

Sophie Williams, former global manager of production planning at Netflix (NFLX), and author of The Glass Cliff: Why Women in Power Are Undermined – And How to Fight Back, has explained why organisations turn to women in moments of crisis.

“There’s a perception that when a team has gone through a hard time, what we are looking for suddenly becomes someone to make us feel better. Someone to play office mum, someone to soothe those experiences and those team members. And not necessarily make transformational change, as they say, but to just make people feel better in that experience,” she said in an earlier interview with Harvard Business Review.

“But because we are not bringing these women in with expectation of transformational changemaking, even when they are capable of it, it means that we don’t often give them either the tools or the time that are necessary to turn that perceived failure into a success before they’re exited. And so we see female leaders being 24% more likely to be fired than their male counterparts. We also see them having significantly shorter tenures in role once they are there,” she said.

The “office adult” label

Bloomberg columnist Beth Kowitt makes a similar point: “If the default for men in tech is charismatic genius, for senior women it is still way too often the office adult.”

Kowitt notes that Sheryl Sandberg, as chief operating officer at Meta Platforms Inc. (META), played the “polished grownup” to counterbalance Mark Zuckerberg’s “hoodie-wearing, college-dropout persona.”

Linda Yaccarino, as CEO of X, had to “clean up the mess left in the wake of Elon Musk.”

The label, she says, implies “a certain kind of executive; one who ensures everyone is well-behaved and on schedule, who brings stability and credibility — but not necessarily big vision.”

“For a generation of women, that may have been the only way in the door,” she says, drawing a comparison with Kress.

Reports that Huang called Kress a “deer in the headlights”, a 'reporting CEO' who could not help him set strategy, have already set a lens through which to view her: as a second fiddle, not thought of much by the rockstar founder-CEO.

To be sure, as Kowitt points out, Kress was hired after Huang interviewed 22 candidates, and said he wanted her to be CFO "for as long as we shall live.”

Kress to run two of the company’s most important jobs

Those who see Kress’s appointment as a glass cliff also point out that she must now run the two most important functions at the company, a daunting task despite Kress' credentials and expertise.

Nvidia is the unofficial financier of the AI boom, spreading its vast cash piles as investments in budding AI startups, including OpenAI and Anthropic, and in ecosystem players such as neoclouds like CoreWeave (CRWV).

Her role as CFO is therefore far from that of a mere bean counter.

Kress is a seasoned executive. She has spent 13 years at Nvidia, after nearly 25 years in finance roles at major technology companies such as Cisco (CSCO), Microsoft (MSFT) and Texas Instruments (TXN).

Even so, does holding both jobs set her up to fail?

“I wouldn’t call holding both roles a set-up on its own. Interim CEOs who keep their CFO role aren’t unheard of,” Cook said.

She pointed to HP (HPQ), which in 2010 named Cathie Lesjak interim CEO in addition to her CFO role after Mark Hurd left.

Lesjak served about three months before the board went outside for its next CEO.

“What concerns me more is authority and support. My work with Dr. Christy Glass found that women CEOs often lack the support or authority to accomplish their strategic goals,” she said.

More recently, Cook said, her research with Glass and Dr Alicia Ingersoll found that women CEOs have shorter tenures than men and are more likely to be dismissed involuntarily.

The gap widens when women are appointed during weak organisational performance.

Authority, loyalty and credit

On the earnings call this week, the board ruled out bringing Huang back, after a massive campaign for his reinstatement backed by shareholders, former and current employees, and supporters including Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump.

But the decision alone will not quickly change sentiment.

Cook also points out that Huang’s family remains inside the company.

His daughter, Madison Huang, holds a senior role, and his son and son-in-law are in leadership positions too.

“If coalitions form around his return, or people simply fail to support her, she is leading without full authority,” she said.

Finally, Cook turns to the financing question.

“Sources describe Kress as potentially more conservative than Huang, and she has sometimes pushed back on deals he championed. If she pulls back and growth slows, she may get the blame. If things go well, the credit may go to the foundation Jensen built."

"In other words, she may get the blame if things go wrong but not the credit if they go right. As one executive in our research put it, ‘If you don’t produce magic in a short period of time, then they say this isn’t working.’”

A baptism by fire

Earlier this week, Kress faced her first earnings call as interim chief rather than just as CFO.

Observers scrutinised not only what she said but also her tone of voice, an early example of the pressure she will face.

Many experts made note that she relied heavily on scripted remarks and sounded robotic and monotone, while some also wrote about her nervousness.

The sceptics

There are, of course, those who reject both the view that Kress’s appointment is a glass cliff and the phenomenon itself.

Last month, a senior McKinsey partner was removed from his leadership roles after LinkedIn posts questioning the phenomenon drew criticism.

Chris Bradley, who is based in Australia, was until recently one of a handful of directors at the McKinsey Global Institute, the consulting firm’s business and economics research arm.

He questioned whether the phenomenon existed at all.

In the now-deleted posts, he called the glass cliff “a very convenient way to always be a victim in the rain.”

On Nvidia specifically, a recent LinkedIn thread on the phenomenon drew a comment from Stan Clark, advisor at Infocrest Solutions and a former senior director at Oracle (ORCL).

“Colette Kress has earned this. Thirteen years as Nvidia’s CFO, through the company’s biggest growth years. She knows the customers, the numbers, and the team,” Clark said.

“Safra Catz showed what a leader with that background can do. She took on the co-CEO role at Oracle, then led the company after Mark Hurd passed away, and she was exceptional. My bet is on Colette. Rooting for her and the whole Nvidia team.”

The CFO-to-CEO trend

Cook says her findings show that glass cliff appointments are often the culmination of a long-term, risk-centred career strategy.

“Because these leaders are highly visible as outsiders but often invisible as leaders, many deliberately take on risky, high-profile assignments throughout their careers to prove their mettle. That pays off, but it comes with what we call a risk tax: a standard of perfection where one mistake can end a career, constant fear of derailment, and real performance fatigue over time,” she says.

The growing trend of CFOs becoming CEOs may also be cited to question whether Kress’s appointment is a glass cliff.

In 2025, 10.26% of sitting CEOs at Fortune 500 and S&P 500 firms came directly from the CFO role, the highest share in a decade, according to Crist Kolder Associates’ 2025 Volatility report, released on Jan. 28.

In 2024, the figure was 7.1%.

Recent corporate moves bear this out.

Toyota (TM) this year appointed CFO Kenta Kon as president and CEO, succeeding Koji Sato.

Unilever (UL) named CFO Fernando Fernandez as CEO, succeeding Hein Schumacher.

“The CFO-to-CEO trend is real. CFO-to-CEO promotions are at a decade high, and those promotions have been internal. So on its face, an internal CFO stepping up fits current practice,” Cook says.

“My sense, though, is that tech firms, and chip companies especially, lean toward leaders with engineering and product backgrounds, so I’m less sure the CFO trend holds as strongly there.”

What happens next

Cook, however, urges a focus on what comes next.

“The bigger point is that you can’t separate the two by looking at the appointment alone. You have to look at what happens next. Is she seriously considered for the permanent role? Is she given the authority and support to actually lead? And if she is replaced, by whom and why?" she says.

"In my work with Dr. Christy Glass, we found that when firm performance declined under women and minority CEOs, they were likely to be replaced by white men, which we call the savior effect. These leaders are given fewer degrees of freedom to lead their firms out of crisis. Lesjak served as a bridge at HP and went back to the CFO role when the board brought in an outsider. Whether Kress follows that path or is genuinely in the running will tell us a lot.”

Meanwhile, Nvidia’s recruitment firm has reportedly approached Rene Haas, CEO of Arm (ARM), in its search for a new chief executive.

Haas spent seven years at Nvidia before joining Arm in 2013. He became Arm’s CEO in 2022 and has since overseen its expansion into the booming AI infrastructure market.

data.title: Nasdaq 100 Tests Major Long-Term Support
data.description:
The Nasdaq 100 (QQQ) is sitting right on a major long-term support level. Holding the $636 to $637 area is crucial for any chance at a short-term bounce. And even if a bounce does come, there’s plenty of resistance stacked up above. The strongest of it is the short-term trend-line off the all-time highs.

How far has the Nasdaq 100 fallen?

QQQ topped out near $763 in early October. It’s now trading around $636, which puts it down roughly 17% from the highs. The Nasdaq 100 officially entered correction territory at the start of the month, and the selling hasn’t let up. Thursday’s 2% drop marked the sixth straight losing day for the S&P 500, and chip stocks fell around the world again overnight.

What stands out most to me is how the market handled Nvidia’s earnings. Nvidia more than doubled its revenue from a year ago and guided higher, and the stock still closed lower the next day. It isn’t uncommon for stocks to do that, but when a market sells off on great earnings, that tells you a lot about where sentiment is, especially when it entered earnings having already been hammered by investors and the stock market as a whole. And still, buyers aren’t in a hurry to step in yet.

Why is the $636 to $637 level so important for QQQ?

It’s the old ceiling. QQQ’s highs in November of last year and again in January both stalled right at this level, and the stock chopped around underneath it for months. It finally broke out in April and never looked back, until now.

That’s the classic setup where old resistance becomes new support, and this is the first time QQQ has come back to test it from above. It matters even more because QQQ already lost its rising trend-line off the April 2025 lows this week. If $636 to $637 gives way too, QQQ falls back inside that old trading range, and the bottom of that range is a long way down.

What resistance levels should you watch if QQQ bounces?

Even if this level holds, a bounce has a lot of work to do:

  1. The $655 to $661 area. This is where the broken trend-line from the April 2025 lows meets the late-July low. Both were support not long ago. Now they’re overhead.

  2. The 200-day moving average, around $683. QQQ sliced through it earlier this month.

  3. The short-term trend-line off the all-time highs. This is the one I’d watch most closely. QQQ has put in a series of lower highs since the October peak, and the line connecting them has capped every rally attempt so far. Until QQQ gets back above it, any bounce is just that, a bounce inside a downtrend.

How I’m trading QQQ here

If QQQ holds this level into the close, I’ll look for a bounce, but I’ll treat it as a trade, not a new uptrend. That means a tight stop just below support, and taking profits as it runs into the $655 to $661 area. I’m not expecting a V-shaped recovery while QQQ is still below that short-term trend-line.

If $636 to $637 breaks (which it is currently doing as of this writing), I stay defensive. There’s no reason to catch a falling knife, and cash is a position too.

It’s also monthly options expiration today, which can add some extra whipsaw, so I’ll wait for the close before reading too much into the intraday moves.

As I always say, Plan your trade, manage your risk, and the profits will take care of themselves.

data.title: Dow Jones Industrial Average Drops For A Fifth Day As AI Rout Widens
data.description:
Five falls in five sessions have taken the Dow Jones Industrial Average more than 10% below its August record close, and the selling is no longer confined to artificial intelligence (AI) stocks. The index dropped to just under 48,000, its lowest since April, and is trading near 48,100. Thursday's close under 50,000 was its first since June, and the run is on track to be its worst week since April 2025.

Nvidia (NVDA), a Dow member, is on track for a seventh straight fall after Reuters reported that Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) enforcement staff are examining its accounting. The shares were lower before the report and doubled the loss after it. The Dow is weighted by share price, so Nvidia near $127 counts for less in it than Goldman Sachs (GS) and Caterpillar (CAT), two of its highest-priced members, which also led the fall.

Anthropic (ANT), whose listing was meant to steady AI stocks, rose 17% on its Thursday debut and traded within 5 cents of its $83 offer price a day later. Fed Governor Cook said September's rate hike wasn't enough to curb inflation, which adds higher borrowing costs to the doubts over AI spending. Walmart (WMT), Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) and Procter & Gamble (PG) rose, which is why the Dow has fallen less than the NASDAQ 100.

On the calendar

US Purchasing Managers Index (PMI) surveys for November come at 14:45 GMT on Monday, before New York Fed President Williams speaks at 21:00 GMT. Traders no longer fully price a Fed hike on December 9, so each Fed speaker now bears on whether one comes at all.

Wednesday, November 25 has October core Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index (PCE) inflation and the first Gross Domestic Product (GDP) figure for the third quarter at 13:30 GMT, then the Fed's Beige Book at 19:00 GMT. US stock markets are shut on Thursday for Thanksgiving.

On the charts

At Friday's low the index had given back about two-thirds of the climb from April's low near 45,000 to August's peak just under 54,750, and the five-session run accounts for most of that fall. During the run it went through its 200-day Exponential Moving Average (EMA), near 50,750, for the first time since April. The 50-day EMA has turned down near 51,750.

data.title: Why Anthropic Could Get Ugly Next Week
data.description:
Anthropic (ANT) touched $83.47 this morning, and it bounced.

That’s no coincidence. Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share on Wednesday, and there’s a buyer sitting at that price whose whole job is to keep the stock from falling apart.

The Buyer With One Job

When a company goes public, one or more of the banks in the underwriting syndicate can act as what’s called a stabilization agent. If the shares start to sell off under the IPO price, the stabilization agent steps in and buys.

The rule is exact. It can’t buy a single share above $83. At $83 and below, it can nibble, and it can take on a lot of risk if this thing starts to come down.

And it’s not some guy behind a screen. It’s a computer system, an algorithm fighting the market at $83. If we hit 83 today, you’ll see it. The stock will come down, and they’ll punch it right back. Come down, punch it right back. I’ve traded around a stabilization algorithm before, about 25 years ago.

How Long Can They Hold The Line?

That depends on whether they have what’s called a green shoe. A green shoe lets the underwriters put more shares out to the market even weeks after the IPO if there’s demand. If they have one, the stabilization agent can stay in there for weeks or even months.

Monday Changes Everything

On Monday, options start trading on Anthropic, and a stabilization agent can’t do very much against an options market.

Right now, you can’t short the stock at home, because there’s no stock in the book to borrow. So traders who want to get short will buy puts, and buy puts, and buy puts. The market maker sells them those puts, then shorts the stock to reduce its own risk, because market makers are allowed to do that.

Once the options list, there’s no stability. This thing could drop to 50.

So set an alert on Anthropic at or below $83 today. If it gets there, watch the tape and see the algorithm punch it back. Then on Monday, watch what happens to that same level when the puts start trading.

data.title: Michael Burry Takes Profits On Nvidia Puts As Chip Stocks Extend Sell-Off
data.description:
Michael Burry, the investor made famous by The Big Short, has taken profits on part of his bearish bets against Nvidia and the semiconductor sector following a sharp technology sell-off this week.

In a Friday update to subscribers of his Cassandra Unchained Substack, Burry said he sold 50% of his put options on Nvidia (NVDA) and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH), locking in what he described as substantial gains.

He retained the remaining half of both positions.

Put options increase in value when the underlying shares decline, allowing investors to profit from falling stock prices.

Burry also reduced some of his bullish exposure, selling roughly one-third of his call options on animal health company Zoetis (ZTS) to secure gains.

However, he left his bearish April 2027 put options on the Nasdaq 100 untouched, maintaining his longer-term negative outlook on large-cap technology stocks.

Burry increases MercadoLibre stake

Alongside the profit-taking, Burry increased his position in Latin American e-commerce company MercadoLibre (MELI) by 20%.

He also pointed to what he described as "absolute relative strength" in several stocks, including healthcare companies Molina Healthcare (MOH) and HCA Healthcare (HCA), software company Adobe (ADBE), and grocery retailer Sprouts Farmers Market (SFM).

The portfolio changes indicate that Burry is adjusting some of his positions following the recent market moves while retaining his bearish exposure to the Nasdaq 100.

His decision to lock in part of his Nvidia and semiconductor ETF gains came as chip stocks endured a difficult week, with Nvidia extending its losing streak despite reporting strong quarterly results.

Nvidia shares extend losing streak

Nvidia shares fell for a seventh consecutive session on Friday and were on track for their worst weekly performance since November 2018.

The decline came despite the chipmaker reporting record quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion, more than double the year-earlier figure.

Net profit increased 109% to $64.9 billion, beating Wall Street forecasts.

Interim CEO Colette Kress also provided a strong outlook, forecasting fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion and raising the company's fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook to 75%.

However, the earnings performance did little to support the stock as investors continued to assess concerns surrounding the company and the broader technology sector.

Nvidia has also faced scrutiny over allegations involving the potential diversion of advanced chips to China.

Two House Democrats reportedly opened an inquiry into whether the company sought to influence the Commerce Department's investigation of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud company suspected of illegally diverting advanced chips to China.

Separately, Representative Brett Guthrie, chairman of the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, sent a letter to Kress requesting that Nvidia officials appear before the panel by December 2.

Semiconductor sell-off weighs on technology stocks

Nvidia's decline spread across the wider semiconductor sector, adding to pressure on technology stocks as investors questioned whether substantial spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure would generate sufficient returns.

The Invesco QQQ ETF (QQQ), which tracks the Nasdaq 100, fell 9% over the week.

Other major chipmakers also recorded steep losses on Friday.

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) dropped more than 11%, while Micron Technology (MU) declined over 13%.

The declines reflected broader concerns about valuations and supply chains across the semiconductor industry.

data.title: Consequences For Excesses?
data.description:
Starting out with a quick follow-up from yesterday, as markets went down a lot again on Friday. Oddly though, the things I follow, more of them were up today in the bigger decline versus yesterday's slightly smaller decline. 

For a long time here and in client letters, we've been talking about obvious excesses in the tech sector while being clear that there was no way to know when or if there would ever be a consequence for those obvious excesses. If there was no way to know when or if there would be consequences, then the only protection was to be underweight versus the index. Zero weight was not/is not practical, but being underweight was/is practical. 

For the last six months, the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) is down 40%, as you can see. Since the beginning of October, SOXX is down 35%. I have no idea what will happen, but that seems awfully fast. I'm not trying to predict anything, more like just read the room. Fast declines tend to snap back quickly, so maybe this one will too?

Where we've spent a lot of time trying to understand autocallable ETFs, this event has been a great chance to learn more about how they behave when markets get hit. Some of the declines have been massive. Those are just Friday's declines.

I was talking to a buddy today who said he's concerned about all the stuff going on with outages and the like. I'm not really concerned that there will be some sort of societal-level breakdown, but similar to COVID, there could certainly be some inconveniences. If you haven't already done so, it's a good idea to add two-factor authentication to all your accounts. There's no reason not to have extra batteries on hand, a little cash in the house, get a little ahead on food (I'm not saying doomsday levels) and for us a little bit of gasoline which is for our ATV and generator. I'd say it's always a good idea to have some level of preparedness for emergencies if you want to think of it that way, or a little less dramatically, preparedness for inconveniences.

The rest of the post from here was written a couple of days ago, but events got in the way. 

The new iShares Macro AlphaBeta Active ETF (GMIX) takes a page out of ReturnStacked's playbook, allocating 100% to large-cap domestic equities and 100% to global macro, so it is leveraged. Here's a write-up from BlackRock in support of the new fund. 

iShares has a newer ETF that is in the macro realm with IALT, and so far, that fund has done pretty well. I saw some chatter, though, that the macro sleeve of GMIX might look more like PBAIX, which is a BlackRock fund I'd never heard of before. PBAIX is a 5-star fund, and it has done well, but I wouldn't say it's done better than some of the other macro funds we've looked at. As I learn more about it, maybe it will turn out that it takes a different path to a similar result as the others, which would make it interesting. 

RDMIX is a ReturnStacked product that, similar to GMIX, has 100% equity/100% macro. The latest incarnation goes back to the start of 2025. The ReturnStacked guys don't suggest 100% or 50% of a portfolio into their funds but the backtest maybe gives a little color on how equities and macro could work together. 

Staying in the macro realm, the other day we mentioned the Victory Pioneer Multi-Asset Income Fund (PMFYX). Despite the name, it is not a straightforward fixed income fund. It is legit multi-asset. Morningstar categorized it as Global Moderate Allocation. This is from the fund's July 30 factsheet.

It goes pretty far afield. A good portion of its high sixes yield comes from equity-linked notes in a similar manner as how JEPI uses equity-linked notes. That is not a precise explanation, but thinking of them as short-term autocallables might give some context. 

This chart is helpful for framing what I think are different objectives. PMFYX isn't really a stand-alone fixed income fund, and it doesn't trade that way. Similar to AQRIX it seems like a potential replacement for VBAIX, so maybe calling it macro isn't fair. PBAIX does look like a replacement for a stand-alone fixed income fund, at least what I think people want bond funds to look like with very low volatility and very shallow drawdowns. It hasn't had a down year in our ten-year backtest.

If you think you want to dabble in macro funds, I would suggest trying to draw a conclusion about what you think it is trying to do. Right or wrong, I don't think PBAIX is a replacement for VBAIX. Right or wrong, PMFYX very well could be...more so than PBAIX anyway.

You can decide for yourself whether the above is compelling or not. There's not much differentiation over time except in 2022. Portfolio 1 was down 6.01% that year; Portfolio 2 was down 8.45% compared to a drop of 16.87% for VBAIX. In other words, it differentiated when investors most needed it to. In 2023, 2024, and 2025, both were very similar to VBAIX, but this year, as bonds have struggled price-wise again, Portfolios 1 and 2 are way ahead again. 

This next chart throws a different type of macro fund into the mix with DYMIX.

It's a shorter lookback because DYMIX is a newer fund. DYMIX looks much different in terms of growth rate, volatility, and drawdowns. Higher growth rates aren't the only determining factor. Anyone who cares about this sort of alternative needs to consider not just the growth rate but how it would fit in with their other holdings. There's no way to know how well they will do in the future for their respective growth rates, but it is reasonable to conclude that PBAIX will be far less volatile than DYMIX.

In terms of correlations, I'd be more confident in PBAIX maintaining its low correlation to VBAIX, but based on DYMIX's volatility, I would expect the correlation to VBAIX to be more volatile too.

data.title: Stocks: Correction, Bear Market, Or Something Much Worse?
data.description:
After several weeks of selling pressure, growing volatility, and significant declines in technology and AI-related stocks, investors are facing an important question: Is this a normal correction, the beginning of a cyclical bear market, or something much worse, similar to what unfolded after the major stock market peaks in 2000 and 2007?

Recent developments involving NVIDIA (NVDA) have added to uncertainty surrounding the AI trade. data.title: Private Credit Redemptions: Why Investors Still Can’t Get Out
data.description:
Private credit redemptions are falling, but most funds still return only 5% of shares per quarter.

Key Takeaways

  • Redemption requests at the largest non-traded private credit funds are easing, but most still pay out only 5% of shares per quarter.

  • At Blue Owl’s flagship OCIC, most third-quarter requests came from investors resubmitting orders that went unfilled earlier in the year.

  • The demand was built when cash paid nothing. In nine of the twelve years from 2010 through 2021, the 3-month T-bill averaged below 0.5%.

  • Listed BDCs, which get a daily market price, trade at a median of about 88 cents per dollar of reported net asset value.

  • The better question for an investor is whether you’ll need the money before the line clears.

The headlines say private credit redemptions are easing. They are. In the third quarter, investors asked to pull $4.2 billion from Blue Owl’s two largest non-traded credit funds, down from $4.7 billion in the second quarter and a record $5.4 billion in the first.1 However, both funds still bought back just 5% of their shares, the same as every other quarter this year. Such is the part of the story most coverage skips. Fewer investors are heading for the exit, but the ones already in line are still standing there.

That matters to anyone who owns one of these funds or got pitched one over the last few years. The pitch was income with “semi-liquid” access. Income has shown up. For a lot of people, access hasn’t.

“Semi-Liquid” Means Liquid Until Everyone Wants Out

Non-traded business development companies (BDCs) and interval funds don’t trade on an exchange. You get out when the fund offers to buy back your shares, usually once a quarter. That offer is typically capped at 5% of shares outstanding. When requests exceed the cap, the fund prorates. In other words, everyone who asks gets the same fraction of their request filled, and the remaining shares stay put.

Ares Strategic Income Fund shows how that works in practice. In its third-quarter tender, investors submitted roughly 50.4 million shares, and the fund bought about 19.3 million of them, or 38.2% of each request.2 Holders with fewer than 100 shares got paid first. Everyone else waited.

Seven of the ten non-traded BDCs tracked by Crowdfunded Wealth prorated their latest completed offering, filling between 12.8% and 49.9% of investors’ requests.3 The three that paid in full simply had fewer people asking. Notice that none of this is a default. The gate is NOT a malfunction. It’s written into the prospectus. And it’s working exactly as designed, which is precisely the issue if you need the cash. A gate that protects the fund from a fire sale, by forcing it to sell loans into a weak market at whatever price a buyer will offer just to meet withdrawals that came in faster than the loans can mature, is the same gate that keeps you from your money. It cuts both ways.

Why Are Private Credit Redemptions Still Being Prorated?

A question that keeps landing in my inbox goes something like this: “If requests are falling, isn’t the problem fixed?” Not quite. Fewer requests mean a shorter line. They don’t mean a wider door.

Look at Blue Owl Credit Income Corp. (OCIC), a $35 billion fund. Requests ran at 21.9% of shares in the first quarter, 18.8% in the second, and 16.8% in the third.1,4 That’s improvement. Yet Reuters reported that most third-quarter requests came from investors resubmitting tenders that hadn’t been filled earlier in the year.1 Such is how a queue works. The people asking to leave in September are largely the same people who asked in June.

For a better understanding of what this means, let’s run the arithmetic. At a 5% quarterly cap, a 16.8% line takes roughly three and a half quarters to clear. That assumes nobody new joins it. OTIC, the smaller tech-heavy sibling, saw requests hold near 39% of shares. At the same pace, that’s nearly two years. Blackstone’s BCRED, the largest of the group, received tenders for about 181 million shares in its third-quarter offer, roughly 10% of shares outstanding. It bought back about 90 million of them, or 49.9% of each request, for $2.13 billion.5

There are exceptions. KKR’s FS Income Trust Select saw requests of 5.06% and paid every one, stretching slightly past its cap.6 That’s a fund with under $1 billion in net assets and a small overage. The arithmetic changes when the line is three times the door.

How TINA Built The Line At The Exit

To understand why the line formed, you have to go back to where the money came from. For most of the decade after the financial crisis, the Fed held short rates near zero. Savers who needed income had two choices: accept nothing on cash or seek “yield” elsewhere. Wall Street called it “TINA,” for “there is no alternative.” It pushed a generation of conservative money further out on the risk curve than it had ever been.

As is always the case, when there is a LOT of investor demand, Wall Street will find a way to capitalize on it. Private credit was the perfect product for that environment. It paid high single-digit to low double-digit distributions. The reported value barely moved because the loans weren’t marked to market every day. Investors saw a “smooth” line and concluded it was safe. That’s the confusion. Low reported volatility and low risk are different things, and illiquidity is the cost that never shows up in the monthly statement. Howard Marks put the general version of this better than anyone:

“The riskiest thing in the world is the widespread belief that there’s no risk.” – Howard Marks, Oaktree Capital Management

Now flip the setup. As of November 12, the 3-month bill yields 4.32%.7 My colleague Michael Lebowitz recently laid out how investors have moved from TINA to TIGA: “there is a good alternative”. When cash pays four percent with daily liquidity, the extra few points from a gated loan fund look a lot less compelling. Some of today’s private credit redemptions reflect credit worry. Much of it, I suspect, is investors doing that math for the first time.

The Strongest Case For Staying In

The other side of this debate has real merit. The underlying loans are mostly performing. At Ares Capital, the largest listed BDC, loans on non-accrual were 2.4% of the portfolio at cost as of September 30, up from 1.8% at year-end but hardly a collapse.8 The Fed called the risks tied to private credit redemptions “manageable” back in May.9 Evercore’s Glenn Schorr said the industry “it appears that the industry has successfully isolated the direct lending wound.”1

The gate also protects the investors who stay. Back in March, I made this case in Subprime Crisis 2.0: Will Private Credit Be The Trigger? Gating and a mostly institutional investor base, I argued, make this look more like a painful credit cycle than a 2008-style collapse. I still think that’s right. Distributions keep arriving while you wait, and nobody is forced to dump loans at distressed prices.

“A gate is a promise kept to the fund. It’s a promise deferred to you.”

So the case for staying is real. The cost is just as real: you’ve handed the timing of your exit to a tender schedule. For an investor with a long horizon and no near-term need for the money, that may be a fair trade. For one who planned on this as a source of spending money, the trade looks very different.

What Listed BDCs Say About Private Credit Redemptions

There’s a useful cross-check here. Listed BDCs hold the same kind of loans to the same kind of middle-market companies. The difference is that they trade on an exchange every day. Their price shows what investors will actually pay for a dollar of those loans today. A non-traded fund’s reported NAV can’t tell you that.

The detail that jumps out is Blue Owl’s own listed BDC, OBDC. It reported a net asset value of $14.32 a share at the end of September and closed November 13 at $10.97, or about 77 cents on the dollar.8,10 Its non-traded siblings transact with redeeming investors at reported NAV, when they transact at all. That doesn’t prove the non-traded marks are wrong. Listed prices carry their own fear premium, and a discount can say as much about sentiment as about the loans. But when the market price and the reported price differ by 10% to 25%, the investor who can only exit at the reported price, 5% at a time, is relying on marks the market won’t confirm.

Buyers are putting their own marks on these loans as well. In November, BC Partners’ listed BCP Investment Corp. agreed to buy Investcorp Credit Management BDC at 90% of its adjusted net asset value. It’s part of a wave of consolidation as smaller lenders look for scale. Ares Capital agreed to acquire MidCap Financial Investment Corp. in late October. When a professional buyer pays 90 cents per dollar of reported loans, that’s information, too.

My colleague Michael Lebowitz walked through why not all BDC yield is created equal, and the same discipline applies here. A discount is information. Deciding whether it’s an opportunity takes more work.

Is Private Credit Safe For Your Portfolio?

The word “safe” is the wrong focus. The much better test is whether the money you invest can sit idle for as long as it takes the line to clear. Start with the timeline. If you may need these funds in the next two years, the queue matters more than the yield. If the money truly is long-term, the gate is an inconvenience rather than a crisis.

More importantly, you should also focus on just how much of your liquid net worth sits behind a gate. A small sleeve of private credit in a large portfolio is one thing. A retirement income plan built around one is something else. Will a tender schedule ever be convenient? No. However, will knowing your exposure keep a gate from becoming a forced decision somewhere else in the portfolio? Absolutely.

Finally, ask what your plan assumes about a bad year. Retirees selling assets during a drawdown already face the problem I described in Sequence of Return Risk: The Math That Breaks Retirements. If the “liquid” sleeve you planned to draw from is gated, you sell whatever else is liquid. Often, that happens at the worst moment. Such is the hidden cost of illiquidity: it rarely hurts the asset that’s locked. It hurts the assets that aren’t.

None of this argues for rushing to tender. It also says nothing about whether any particular fund is a good or bad holding for you. It argues for knowing exactly what you own: the tender calendar, the cap, how proration works, and how long your share of the line might take to clear. Right now, the consensus says the private credit scare is over. It may be. The line is still there either way.

Bottom Line

Private credit redemptions are easing, but the 5% door hasn't widened, so any money behind a gate should be money you won't need until the line clears.

The yield was real. So was the lockup, and plenty of investors are only now reading that part of the brochure.

Questions This Article Answers

Why can't I withdraw my money from a private credit fund?

Most non-traded BDCs and interval funds buy back shares once a quarter, and cap repurchases at about 5% of shares outstanding. When redemption requests exceed that cap, the fund prorates, filling only part of each request. In their latest completed offers, seven of the ten non-traded BDCs tracked by Crowdfunded Wealth filled between 12.8% and 49.9% of requests.

What does proration mean in a private credit tender offer?

Proration means every investor who asked to redeem gets the same percentage of their request filled. In Ares Strategic Income Fund’s third-quarter 2026 tender, about 50.4 million shares were submitted and about 19.3 million were bought, so investors received 38.2% of their request after holders of fewer than 100 shares were paid first. The rest of the shares stay in the fund until a later tender.

Is private credit safe right now?

The underlying loans are mostly performing, and redemption requests have eased since the first quarter of 2026. The bigger risk for individual investors is liquidity. If you may need the money before your place in the redemption line clears, a gated fund can force you to sell other assets at a bad time.

How long does it take to get out of a non-traded BDC?

It depends on how long the line is relative to the 5% quarterly cap. A fund with requests equal to 16.8% of shares, as Blue Owl’s OCIC saw in the third quarter of 2026, would need roughly three and a half quarters to clear the line if no new requests arrived. A fund with requests for nearly 39% of its shares would need almost two years.

  2. Ares Strategic Income Fund, Schedule TO-I/A final amendment, September 25, 2026.

ADS (33.9%) confirmed by AltStreet. HLEND and NHPIF (43.7%) confirmed by AltsWire, November 4, 2026.

  5. Blackstone Private Credit Fund final tender results (filed November 2, 2026), reported by Blue Vault and AltsWire: 181,287,647 shares tendered, 90,421,325 purchased (about 49.9%), $2.13 billion at the September 30 NAV of $23.51 per share.

  7. U.S. Treasury yield data via Massive Market Data, daily 3-month yields January 2010 through November 12, 2026. Annual figures are simple averages of daily observations. 2026 is a partial year.

Poland will release industrial output, labour market and retail sales data, while Czech confidence indicators are expected to show weaker consumer sentiment but a modest improvement in business confidence

Poland: Industrial weakness persists as consumption loses momentum

October industrial output and labour market data will be released on Monday. Fewer working days than in October 2025 mean that we should expect low-single-digit annual growth in industrial output, as the underlying trend remains lacklustre and uneven. Cost pressures in industry are mounting, pushing producer prices (PPI) higher. Recent readings suggest that price pressures not only stem from rising refining prices but are becoming increasingly broad-based. Nevertheless, this has not translated into stronger pressure on core consumer prices, as weak demand is forcing businesses to compress margins.

The labour market has stabilised, with wage growth in the enterprise sector slowing to below 6% year-on-year and employment continuing to decline. With demand for labour somewhat weaker, supply-side deterioration, reflecting the shrinking working-age population, is playing an increasingly dominant role. The unemployment rate remains low and among the lowest in the European Union.

October retail sales data follow on Tuesday. Fewer trading days and a high reference base for food sales will outweigh some recovery in fuel sales following another cut in VAT and excise duty on gasoline. We also see limited room for stronger sales of durable goods, which have proved surprisingly resilient to the strain on household finances from higher fuel bills and slowing wage growth. Consumption is projected to weaken further in the coming quarters as elevated uncertainty keeps the propensity to save high.

Czech Republic: Consumer confidence likely weakened on higher food prices

Consumer confidence likely deteriorated in November, with Tuesday's release expected to reflect the impact of rising food prices. That said, the consumer mood likely remained solidly above its long-term average, as households continue to benefit from decent nominal and real wage dynamics. In contrast, business confidence likely edged up in the same month, somewhat correcting its previous pronounced losses while remaining below its long-term average, pressured by rising input costs and ongoing uncertainty.

This week in retail

Walmart (WMT) delivered another robust quarter, exceeding earnings, revenue, and same store sales (SSS) expectations. Earnings increased 4.8% from a year ago, while revenue rose 5.2%. U.S. comparable sales increased 2.9%, although the result was affected by federal Medicare drug-pricing rules. Excluding that impact, comparable sales would have risen approximately 3.6%, suggesting underlying consumer demand was stronger than the headline figure indicates.

Sales growth was broad-based across categories, supported by continued market-share gains and a 23% surge in U.S. e-commerce, driven by strong pickup and delivery demand. The results reinforce a key theme this earnings season: consumers are still spending, but they are shopping more strategically. Both customer traffic and average ticket increased, while Walmart continued to gain market share across income groups, including households earning more than $100,000 annually. This suggests that value-seeking behavior is extending beyond lower-income shoppers, as even higher-income consumers become increasingly selective about where they spend.

E-commerce remains a particularly powerful growth engine. Walmart’s 23% digital growth reinforces a broader trend across retail, with Target (TGT), Home Depot (HD), and Lowe’s (LOW) also reporting strong online sales. data.title: Progress Isn’t Protection
data.description:
This week, Microsoft (MSFT)’s Outlook service went down. A software problem disrupted banking transactions at JPMorgan Chase (JPM) and other major banks. And apparently one router in Arkansas triggered an air traffic control communications failure that brought departures across the country to a halt.

Meanwhile, in China, a battery-powered aircraft designed to carry 19 passengers completed its first flight with a crew aboard.

Extraordinary progress. Surprisingly fragile systems.

Those aren’t contradictory descriptions of the world we live in. They’re increasingly descriptions of the same world.

Consider Equinor (EQNR), the Norwegian energy company. As of Thursday, it was still working to contain a cyberattack. Yet the company’s oil and gas production was running normally, with no indication that data had been stolen or altered.

That’s an important distinction. Resilience doesn’t always mean preventing something from going wrong. Sometimes it means keeping the essential things working while you deal with what went wrong.

The electric aircraft offers a different lesson. China’s CE-25A flew about 37.5 miles with two pilots and a flight-test engineer aboard. It’s an engineering milestone. Just last week, a noted energy analyst told me battery-powered airplanes would never work at scale. This flight doesn’t settle that argument. A successful test and a commercially viable airline service are very different things.

Source: Gulf News

Still, it is worth paying attention to. The fact that it happened in China gives me another reason to reflect on what I saw during my recent visit.

The world is gaining extraordinary capabilities. But as we are learning, adding capabilities and reducing vulnerabilities aren’t necessarily the same thing.

Efficiency Isn’t Resilience

For decades, the global economy rewarded efficiency. The push was to make things wherever they’re cheapest, keep inventories lean, and automate what you can. For the most part, that approach worked.

Spare capacity costs money was the thinking of the day. So do backup suppliers and alternative ways of getting things done. When everything works, those costs are easy to question. When something fails, you discover what they were buying you.

Efficiency and resilience aren’t opposites. A well-run business needs both. The problem comes when we squeeze out every inefficiency without asking whether some of it serves a purpose.

The same question applies to countries. And, as I’ll get to in a moment, to you and me.

Still Connected. More Cautious.

This week’s APEC summit in Shenzhen offers a useful reminder that competing with another country and doing business with it are not mutually exclusive.

Mainstream media focused on Xi Jinping, Donald Trump, and Vladimir Putin sitting at the same table, discussing limits to nuclear weapons.  Those talks were taking place alongside an economic gathering with a different emphasis. At APEC, Xi called for more open trade, closer regional integration, and cooperation in artificial intelligence. I wouldn’t confuse that with an end to strategic competition. Nor would I confuse strategic competition with an end to trade.

The more useful question is where countries are willing to depend on one another—and where they want alternatives.

That’s how I think about resilience. Not complete self-sufficiency, not walking away from every relationship that carries risk. Rather, understanding which dependencies could leave you exposed and deciding what to do about them.

Shenzhen is an unusually good place to think about that question. It was the final stop on my eight-day trip through mainland China’s top-tier cities a few weeks ago.

A recent Bloomberg report describes the city as a showcase for China’s technological ambitions: Huawei, BYD (BYDDF), DJI, robotics, and artificial intelligence. It also describes a less comfortable side of the story—pressure on business profits and workers who aren’t sharing equally in the prosperity.

One parcel delivery worker told Bloomberg his monthly income had fallen from roughly 15,000 yuan a few years ago to about 9,000 yuan. That’s a substantial decline in a city producing some of the world’s most advanced technology.

One worker’s experience isn’t a measure of an entire economy. Nor does it establish that technology caused his pay to fall. But put those two pictures side by side: remarkable industrial capabilities and a household getting by on less.

Technological leadership and household financial security are not the same thing. Which brings up a question: What happens when a country becomes more resilient, but the people living inside it don’t?

Governments and large companies can devote enormous resources to securing supplies, developing alternatives, and protecting essential operations.

Individuals don’t always have that luxury.

The ability to adapt to change looks very different depending on whether you have savings, flexibility, and rising income—or are working harder to cover the same bills. That raises bigger questions about wages, work, and who benefits from technological progress.

There is a narrower question we can do something about today: How much of our financial life depends on everything working exactly as it should?

One phone. One email account. One bank. One copy of an important document.

We can’t control the pace of technological change or the relationship between Washington and Beijing. But we can identify a few points of failure in our own lives, and give ourselves alternatives.

I’m not suggesting you build a bunker, but if the world’s biggest powers are focusing on resilience, what does the same exercise look like for you and me?  

Here’s where I would start.

Protect Your Access

First and foremost, use strong, unique passwords for your important accounts. A password manager makes that much more manageable.

Strong passwords are the starting point, not the whole strategy. Turn on the strongest authentication your provider offers. Where available, phishing-resistant options such as security keys provide stronger protection than relying on a password alone.

Then learn how account recovery works. I can tell you from firsthand experience: The time to figure out how to regain control of an important account is well before you lose access. Once you are locked out, you are operating from a position of weakness. Not fun.

Keep recovery codes somewhere secure that you can reach even if your phone is unavailable. Think through the obvious question: If my phone disappeared tomorrow, how would I get back in?

Protect your phone number, too. Ask your carrier how to block unauthorized SIM changes and transfers of your number to another carrier. These aren’t necessarily the same setting. Verizon (VZ) and AT&T (T) both offer SIM Protection and Number Lock features.

And give your wireless account the same attention you give your financial accounts.  Using a lame password to protect your wireless account is an invitation to a world of trouble.

Keep Your Own Records

Download your financial institutions’ monthly statements, including holdings and share counts—not just a screenshot of the balance.

Keep copies of your insurance policies and other important documents somewhere you can reach them if your usual account or device is unavailable.

The key is not to create another single point of failure.

A copy on the laptop next to you isn’t much help if both copies disappear with the laptop. And an external drive attached to your computer is not an offline backup.

Keep a secure backup somewhere other than your house. At least one backup should also be disconnected from your computer when it isn’t being updated. Occasionally check that you can actually restore the files. A backup and process that you’ve never tested is an assumption, not a plan.

Have an Alternative

Governments and large companies often maintain more than one supplier. Consider applying that same thinking to your financial life.

If your day-to-day banking runs through one institution, a second banking relationship may be worth considering. The point isn’t to predict which bank might have a problem. It’s to avoid having every option depend on the same system.

Have some cash on hand.  In our increasingly cashless society, a stash of $20s can get you out of a short-term jam, be it cyber, weather, or institutional in nature.

Review your insurance with the same mindset. Ask what is covered, what is excluded, and where you may be assuming protection you don’t actually have.  For example, do you have cyber coverage, and if not, should you? Don’t wait until it’s too late to find out.

Make a Family Plan

Precautions are less useful if only one person in the household knows how they work.

Make sure your spouse or another trusted person knows where to find essential information and what to do if you’re unavailable.

Have a safe word or phrase that you, your spouse, and your kids know but never share.  Don’t email it to each other.  Set the safe word in person.  This is a way to verify identity if you get an unexpected request for money. Its purpose is to give everyone permission to pause and verify, rather than act under pressure. Keep the plan simple enough that your family will remember it when they’re worried or distracted.

A Little Preparation Goes a Long Way

The goal here isn’t to anticipate every possible failure. It’s to make sure one failure doesn’t become five.

I’m enthusiastic about what technology can do. What I saw in China gave me plenty to think about. I expect the coming years to bring advances that improve our lives in ways we haven’t yet imagined. I also expect the advances to come at us more and more quickly, and that can cause problems.

data.title: Palo Alto Networks Stock Soars On Strong FCF Guidance - Any More Upside Left In PANW?
data.description:
Palo Alto Networks (PANW), a cybersecurity software subscription company, reported strong free cash flow (FCF) margins and guided to 38% this fiscal year. PANW stock rose 8% on this guidance on Thursday after rising ahead of the results. Could it be worth more?

PANW is at $364.77, up more than 7.0% midday on Thursday, Nov. 19, after rising 9.9% on Wednesday from a recent low of $309.29 on Nov. 17 ahead of the Nov. 18 fiscal Q1 2027 earnings release (ending Oct. 31) after the market closed.

PANW stock - last 3 months - Barchart - Nov. 19, 2026

Moreover, analysts seem to be very positive on the stock. For example, Yahoo! Finance reports that the average price target (PT) of 54 analysts is $405.78, and Barchart's mean survey PT is $398.62. These PTs are only about 8% higher than Thursday's price (11/19).

So, is there much upside left in PANW?

FCF performance and high FCF Margin Guidance

Palo Alto Networks' fiscal Q1 revenue was up 39.25% YoY, and over the past year it rose 30.29%, according to Stock Analysis data.

Moreover, its adjusted free cash flow (FCF rose 13.1% to $1.937 billion YoY. However, its adj. FCF margin fell from 69.2% in Q1 last year to 59.6% in fiscal Q1 2027.

Nevertheless, on a trailing 12-month (TTM) basis (which is important since many of its clients renew subscriptions annually), the adj. FCF rose almost $1 billion from last year.

This can be seen on page 31 of its presentation deck. It shows that TTM adj. FCF rose from $3.75 billion last year to $4.638 billion in Q1 (+23.5%). It was even 5% higher than the Q4 TTM figure.

Palo Alto Networks - Adj. FCF trailing 12 months (TTM) - Q1 deck page 31 - Nov. 18, 2026

Note, however, that the TTM adj. FCF margin dipped slightly to 37.3% from 39.3% of revenue last year and even 38.4% in fiscal Q4.

However, management provided a 38.0% adj. FCF guidance for the year ending July 31, 2027. Let's see how that might work out. 

Forecasting FCF and Price Targets

Management expects its revenue to be between $14.52 billion and $14.57 billion. That's even higher than prior analysts' average forecasts of $14.4 billion.

For the next year, these analysts forecast $16.47 billion in revenue. So, over the next 12 months (NTM), revenue could be about $15 billion:

  $14.55b x 0.75 + $16.47b x 0.25 = $10.91b +$4.12b = $15.02 billion NTM revenue

So, applying a 38% margin, adj. FCF could hit $5.708 billion

That's over $1 billion higher than the $4.638 billion TTM figure shown above. In other words, its forecasted NTM adj. FCF could rise over 23%.

That certainly shows why the stock is up so much. But, how much is left?

For example, Palo Alto Networks' adj. FCF yield has averaged about 2.0% over the last year (i.e., a 50x multiple). So, applying this metric to its NTM adj. FCF forecast:

  $5.708 / 0.02 = $285.4 billion fair value

That's only about 2.5% above its present market cap of $278.32 billion today. And that implies a PT of $372.30. That's lower than other analysts' targets, as I showed above.

Even with a slightly better 1.85% FCF yield (i.e., a 54x multiple), the stock is worth just $308.54 billion, or +10.9% higher. That gives it a NTM price target of $402.81.

Summary and Conclusion

Palo Alto Networks produced strong adj. FCF with lower quarterly margins, including slightly lower TTM adj. FCF as a percent of revenue (37.3%). As a result, with management's guidance of 38% margin this year and applying this to a next 12-month (NTM) revenue forecast, its adj. FCF could hit $5.7 billion.

With a generous 54x multiple, that only implies a 10.9% higher price target for Palo Alto Networks. Nevertheless, the stock could exceed this at any time. 

But value investors have to take this into account when deciding whether its recent rise leaves any upside.

data.title: GM Backs $550 Million Solar Investment In Largest Clean Energy Deal To Date
data.description:
General Motors (GM) announced its largest clean energy investment to date, with the automotive giant signing a deal for 276 MW of energy, serving as the primary customer for two new solar facilities in Michigan developed by NorthStar Clean Energy.

According to GM, the new projects represent a combined investment of approximately $550 million, and are expected to generate roughly 539,000 megawatt-hours of electricity annually.

The new agreements follow an announcement earlier this year by GM that it had secured enough renewable energy to match 100% of electricity consumption across its U.S. facilities in 2025, becoming the first U.S. automaker to reach the milestone.

Under the new deal, GM will serve as the primary customer through a virtual power purchase agreement (VPPA) for the Branch Solar project in Branch County and Lake Iris Solar project in St. Clair County.

According to GM, the facilities are expected to generate electricity equivalent to the combined annual electricity consumption of three of the company’s Michigan assembly plants, Factory ZERO, Flint Assembly and Lansing Delta Township Assembly.

GM said that it plans to apply renewable energy credits generated by the projects toward emissions associated with electricity purchased for its manufacturing operations. The company added that it has reduced its Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas emissions by 52% since 2018.

Casandra Garber, Chief Sustainability Officer, GM, said:

“For GM, long-term renewable energy helps us manage costs, strengthen the operations behind the vehicles, batteries, and technologies we build, and advance our zero-emissions vision. It’s a practical example of how sustainable business and economic growth can reinforce each other.”

data.title: Preliminary Regional Fed Manufacturing Reports Suggest Inflation Is Spreading Downstream
data.description:
In discussing the ISM manufacturing index several weeks ago, I concluded that it “reminded me of the regional Fed reports for the last month, which suggested that while the expansion is intact, the second derivative may be declerating, i.e., the rate of growth has been peaking; and further that its inflationary component is accelerating, which is not good for downstream consumer prices.”

Here’s what the new orders component of that index looked like:

Well, now we have three regional Fed bank reports for November: New York, Philadelphia, and Kansas City, which give us our first look at how manufacturing is doing this month. The first two do get picked up by FRED, so let’s see what their averages can tell us.

First of all, the headline numbers (bue) declined -6.2 to 7.0, which suggests at least that the growth rate is stabilizing and possibly decelerating somewhat.  But, unlike the ISM report at the beginning of this month, the average of the new orders component (red) was the lowest since last year, as it decelerated sharply, by -12.4, to 1.3:

Meanwhile, the respective numbers from the Kansas City Fed constrasted significantly, as the headline regional index rose 7 to 18, and the new orders component rose 13 to 16.

Put all three together and the picture is of a stabilizing topline, and at very least the proverbial bloom might be coming off the rose somewhat as to new orders.

There might be an even more significant amplification present is in the prices component, and specifically prices received from downstream customers (red in the graph below). Prices paid declined -1.3 to 52.0, suggesting the torrid spread of price increases in that component has persisted. But even more signficantly, prices received rose 1.2 to 37.1. The last two months have been the highest readings in that entire series since the start of the Millennium outside of the post-pandemic period:

The regional Kansas City index suggested the same, with prices paid declining -17 to 53, and prices received rising 4 to 30.

In short, producers appear more determined, and able, to pass on higher prices to downstream customers, suggesting that consumer inflation, at least in the goods sector, is not going to slow in the next several months, and may even increase further. And keep in mind that real aggregate nonsupervisory payrolls may go negative YoY as early as next month if there is such a pass-through of inflation and a tepid employment report. In that regard, the best news in the surveys was that employment average rose 5.4 to 1.8:

All well and good for the present, but if corporate profits come under pressure, and real wages come under pressure as well, needless to say that would not be good.

Lower energy costs have therefore provided little relief. Tariffs and rising technology costs may keep underlying inflation elevated even as cheaper oil reduces energy expenses. A stronger dollar also raises its cost in other currencies.

Christopher Waller also raised the possibility of a half percentage point increase or faster subsequent tightening. These messages support the dollar and limit gold recoveries.

The BEA will release October PCE inflation data on November 25. A monthly core reading above the expected 0.3% could support expectations for December and January rate increases. A reading of 0.1% or less could reduce those expectations and support gold. Preliminary November business surveys will also influence the dollar. If Fed officials push back against faster rate increases, gold could find additional support.

Gold Breaks below Weekly Descending Triangle Support

The gold chart below shows a descending triangle with a falling upper boundary and a horizontal base around $3,850 to $4,000. Gold failed to remain above this support area and continued to move lower. The red circle marks the final recovery attempt near the triangle floor. The large weekly decline extends below the former support range. This breakdown shifts attention toward lower historical support levels.

A stable base around these levels could support a recovery, while further declines would keep the outlook negative.

Any recovery initially faces resistance around $3,850 to $4,000. Gold must regain this former support area and remain above it to weaken the breakdown signal. The falling trendline marks the next resistance area as it slopes toward $4,200. A sustained move above that boundary would provide stronger evidence of a trend change. Until then, recoveries may remain vulnerable to renewed declines.

Gold Outlook: Downside Risks Persist Ahead of PCE Inflation

Gold retains a negative outlook as Fed tightening expectations and the weekly triangle breakdown point in the same direction. The immediate downside references are $3,500 and approximately $3,450. Stronger inflation could increase pressure on these levels. Softer data may support a recovery, but lasting technical improvement requires gold to reclaim $3,850 to $4,000. The response to PCE inflation will help determine whether the decline extends or begins to stabilize.

data.title: The Euro Takes A Priced-In Hike Into A Week That Belongs To American Inflation
data.description:
1.1000 has turned EUR/USD back in each of the past three sessions, and it did so in a week when most of the news leaned the Euro's way. Eurozone core inflation was revised higher, the ZEW sentiment survey beat its forecast, and the US factory numbers missed. The pair trades just above 1.0950 regardless, its lowest in 19 months, and has gone nowhere since Monday's break of the round number.

Good news for the Euro bought nothing above 1.1000

Eurostat's final October figures on Wednesday put core inflation at 2.6% YoY, up from a first estimate of 2.5%, and confirmed the headline rate at 4.0%. Tuesday's ZEW survey of economic sentiment came in at 26.5 against a 19.1 forecast. Traders put the odds of a European Central Bank (ECB) hike on December 17 above 90%, a move that would take the deposit rate from 2.50% to 2.75%.

The pair made its low for the year on the day of the inflation revision. A hike that's more than 90% priced has less than 10% left to add to a currency, so stronger inflation data now confirms a decision the market has already traded.

The Fed voted to hold and has argued about hiking ever since

The US calendar leaned the Euro's way as well. The Empire State and Philadelphia Fed factory surveys both came in at less than half their forecasts, industrial production fell 0.4% in October, and weekly jobless claims rose to 203K.

The Dollar didn't need the data. Minutes of the Fed's October meeting, released on Wednesday, showed almost all officials expect further hikes and a couple open to more than a quarter-point in December, and Fed Governor Waller asked for a half-point the same day. The Fed's rate is 3.75%-4.00% against the ECB's 2.50%, a gap of at least 1.25 points before either moves. October's vote was 10-2 to hold, both dissenters wanted a hike, and the committee has spent November debating how quickly to do what it voted not to do.

A December hike raises France's bill too

An ECB hike doesn't land evenly across the bloc. The extra yield investors demand to hold French 10-year debt over Germany's reached about 1.6 points earlier in November, the widest since the Eurozone debt crisis, and France's 2027 budget is still being fought over in parliament. Bank of France Governor Moulin said on Friday that France faces a budget crisis and is in a very different situation from Greece, the second time since early October he has raised the comparison in order to dismiss it.

For EUR/USD, higher ECB rates lift the yield on holding Euros and the cost of rolling French debt at the same time, which may be why a well-flagged hike hasn't put a floor under the pair. European Union (EU) leaders meet on November 26 and 27 with that budget fight unresolved.

PMIs, then PCE, then an account of a meeting already traded

The Hamburg Commercial Bank (HCOB) Purchasing Managers Index (PMI) surveys for November are due on Monday at 09:00 GMT, after a composite reading of 51.7 in October, with the US versions at 14:45 GMT. ECB Chief Economist Lane speaks the same day at 14:30 GMT.

Wednesday at 13:30 GMT is the release that matters most to the pair: October core Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation, forecast at 3.2% YoY after 3.1%, alongside a first estimate of third-quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP) forecast at 3.5% annualized. Traders pared their December Fed bets on Friday as US stocks sold off, so a core number at or above forecast could rebuild them and take the pair through 1.0950. A miss would hand the Euro a second look at 1.1000 with the Fed's preferred measure on its side.

US markets are shut on Thursday for Thanksgiving, which leaves the ECB's account of its October 29 meeting, due at 12:30 GMT, to a thin market. The account will show how close the Governing Council came to hiking in October, which is detail about a decision traders have already made on its behalf.

Technical levels

Resistance: 1.1000 has capped three straight sessions, with each high within about 10 pips of it. Above it, 1.1050 is where the pair paused on November 12 and 13 before breaking lower, and 1.1100 is the October floor it fell through on November 11.

Support: Wednesday's low just above 1.0950 is the 19-month low and has held on both sessions since. There's no 2026 level beneath it on the daily chart, which leaves 1.0900 as the next round number.

Bias: The lean is short while the pair stays under 1.1000. A daily close below 1.0950 targets 1.0900 first and 1.0850 after it. The daily Stochastic Relative Strength Index (Stoch RSI) is in the mid-40s and falling, so momentum isn't stretched enough to argue for a bounce on its own. A daily close above 1.1050 would put the pair back in the range it broke, and the short case ends there.

data.title: Lagarde Sees A €23 Billion Opportunity: Can Tokenization Finally Unite Europe’s 27 Markets?
data.description:
European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde said on Friday, November 20, that tokenization could give Europe something it has chased for decades: one market for financial assets instead of 27. She warned that the chance may not last, because the market is growing fast and its rules are still being written.

She made the case in a keynote at the Frankfurt European Banking Congress. She told the room it was her eighth speech there as ECB President, and her last.

Tokenization means issuing assets such as bonds, shares or fund units as digital tokens on a blockchain, where they can be traded and settled in one place. Europe’s own digital money, though, is still tiny next to the dollar’s. We compared euro and dollar stablecoins to see how far behind it is.

Lagarde Calls Tokenization a Chance for a Single Market

Lagarde spent most of the speech on why Europe acts too late on slow-moving problems. Tokenization was one of three areas where she said the ECB had tried to act early. The other two were the digital euro and the euro’s role abroad.

“With the right framework, tokenisation offers a chance to build a genuine single market in digital assets, integrated from the start. For Europe, that is a huge opportunity,” she said in the speech published by the ECB.

The catch is timing. Lagarde said the global market for tokenized assets was worth around €23 billion in March, five times its size a year earlier. As it grows, its standards will set.

She warned that if standards develop separately, the market could split into platforms that follow different rules and cannot settle with one another. Europe’s stock and bond markets already work that way, with separate national systems that have proved very hard to merge.

Pontes and Appia Are the ECB’s Tokenization Tools

The ECB has already built part of the plumbing. In September, it launched Pontes, a link that lets tokenized trades settle in central bank money, the safest form of money there is, on Eurosystem systems. Every platform can now use the same settlement asset.

Earlier this month, the European Stability Mechanism, the euro area’s rescue fund, settled a €1 billion bond issued directly as a token on Pontes.

A second project, Appia, is working with banks and other firms on common standards for an integrated European market. But Lagarde said the central bank cannot finish the job alone. “Infrastructure alone is not enough. Common rules will be needed too, and those lie with legislators,” she said.

Euro Stablecoins Are Small Next to Dollar Tokens

Stablecoins are tokens pegged to a currency, and they are the cash leg of most crypto and tokenized trades today. On that front, Europe is far behind.

Dollar stablecoins in circulation total about $283.7 billion, while euro stablecoins total about $815 million. That is $1 in euro tokens for every $348 in dollar tokens, or a 0.29% share.

The euro side is growing faster from its small base. Since the stablecoin rules in the EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) law took effect on June 30, 2024, euro stablecoins have grown 244%, while dollar stablecoins grew 76%. That doubled the euro’s share, from 0.15% to 0.29%.

One issuer dominates. Circle’s EURC accounts for about 62% of the euro total, ahead of SG-Forge’s EURCV.

This is why the ECB wants tokenized trades in Europe to settle in central bank money rather than in private tokens. In a market run on dollar stablecoins, European tokenization would depend on a currency the ECB does not control.
