data.title: The Big Picture: When The Math Finally Breaks
data.description:
If you’ve been listening to our broadcast over the years, you know I often remind our listeners of an old rule of thumb: Wall Street is paid to sell you the next hot story, but math is the only thing that never lies.

Right now, the financial press is obsessed with the AI bust and the Fed’s next move. Will they raise rates a quarter or half a point in December? Will that be followed by further hikes in January and March? Currently, the futures market is forecasting a 97% quarter-point increase in December, a 70% quarter-point hike in January, and a 46% quarter-point rise in March. But the market is probably going to force a pivot.

If you step back from the current headlines and look at the big picture, the more important story isn’t really about the Fed or even AI. It’s that the U.S. government is heading straight into a wall of debt refinancing in 2027—and the numbers simply no longer add up.

The 2027 Debt “Maturity Wall”

Imagine a family that went on a massive spending spree back in 2020. Fortunately for them, the bank offered a special introductory promotion: zero-percent interest for five years.

For five years, that family felt rich. They bought whatever they wanted, and their monthly credit card statement looked tiny because their interest rate was practically zero.

Then the promotion ends. The teaser rate expires, and the bank informs them that their borrowing rate is now adjusting to 22%.

Suddenly, even if they don’t buy another single thing, their monthly interest payment alone eats up half their paycheck.

Sound familiar? What happened to homeowners in the 2000s is precisely what is now happening to the U.S. government.

During the 2020–2021 pandemic crisis, the Treasury borrowed trillions of dollars at rock-bottom rates between 0.5% and 1.8%.

Now those 5-year and 7-year IOUs are coming due.

Through the rest of this year, over $1.1 trillion in older, low-rate debt has to be paid off and replaced with brand-new debt.

In 2027, the dam really breaks: approximately $3.4 trillion in medium- and long-term notes come due. When you include short-term Treasury bills, the government will have to roll over close to $9 trillion in a single year.

Here’s the catch: the Treasury can’t borrow at 1% anymore. Today, it must pay close to 5% or more.

For twenty-five years, whenever Uncle Sam rolled over old debt, it did so at lower rates. Monthly payments went down. Today, that dynamic has flipped. Refinancing that mountain of debt at today’s rates adds tens of billions of dollars every single year to the deficit purely through higher interest costs.

The Snowball Effect: Looking at the Real Numbers

In fiscal year 2026, total government spending topped $7.4 trillion. But look at where that money went: net interest on the national debt jumped over 11% to roughly $1.14 trillion. Net interest is now bigger than our entire national defense budget.

Entitlements are on autopilot: Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid ate up another huge chunk of the budget.

According to the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO), our total national debt is blowing past $40 trillion this year. By 2030, debt held by the public will cross 108% of GDP.

To put that into historical perspective: the highest debt level America ever reached was 106% of GDP in 1946, right after mobilizing the entire nation to fight and win World War II. We are on track to permanently shatter that wartime record in peacetime—with no world war, no national draft, and no emergency mobilization.

By 2036, the CBO projects interest payments alone will cross $2.1 trillion a year. At that point, Social Security, healthcare programs, and interest on the debt will consume virtually every single penny of federal taxes collected. Every other department—from the military to the FBI to national parks—will have to be put on the national credit card.

Why Washington Won’t Fix It

You might ask: won’t politicians in Washington just cut spending or raise taxes to fix this?

I’ve watched Washington for over forty years in my career. Neither party has the stomach for real fiscal discipline.

When you look at the major spending proposals on Capitol Hill—whether it’s expanded family tax credits, universal childcare subsidies, healthcare expansions, or housing grants—we are looking at another $3.6 to $4.4 trillion in gross spending programs over the next decade.

Even if you pass every proposed tax increase on corporations and high earners, it barely makes a dent against the compounding wave of interest and baby-boomer retirements. The structural annual deficit will still run at nearly 6% of GDP as far as the eye can see.

The Economy Today: A Tale of Two Consumers

Now let’s look at the economy. Are we about to fall into a deep recession tomorrow?

The economic indicators we watch—like the Conference Board’s Leading Economic Index (LEI)—are actually telling us that growth is holding up around 2%. The job market isn’t falling off a cliff.

Instead, we have a two-track, K-shaped economy.

The Strained Main Street Consumer: If you make an average paycheck, life feels expensive. Prices are up anywhere from 30% to 50% (or higher) since 2020. Credit card debt is at record highs, car loan delinquencies are climbing, and mortgage rates above 7% have frozen the housing market.

The Booming Industrial and AI Pipeline: On the other side of the tracks, money is pouring into artificial intelligence data centers, rebuilding our aging electrical power grid, domestic energy production, and military manufacturing.

This capital-spending boom is keeping the economy afloat. But it has a weak spot: it requires enormous amounts of cheap electricity, expensive equipment, and heavy borrowing. If interest rates stay high, those big corporate projects will eventually hit a wall, too.

The Big Question: When Does the Fed Blink?

Wall Street consensus says the Fed will start cutting rates by mid-2027 because inflation will magically drift down to its 2% target.

I don't buy that inflation story, and neither do many of the sharp macro thinkers we follow.

They point out that the Fed is trapped in a condition economists call Fiscal Dominance. In plain English: the government’s debt has grown so massive that the central bank can no longer control the steering wheel.

Think about the trap Fed Chairman Warsh is in.

If he keeps rates high to fight inflation, he bankrupts the Treasury by forcing them to refinance trillions of dollars at 5%, while crushing regional banks and corporate borrowers.

If he slashes rates, he pours gasoline on inflation, crude oil spikes higher, and consumer prices take off again.

Furthermore, Luke Gromen points out an incredible paradox: when debt is this high, high interest rates fuel inflation. Why? Because the federal government is paying out over $1.1 trillion in cash interest directly into the financial system, putting fresh purchasing power right back into circulation!

So, what happens next? Grant Williams describes it as a forced capitulation. The Fed won’t cut rates because they “won” the inflation fight. No, they will cut rates because the Treasury market will force them to.

We’ve seen this movie before. In the late 1940s, after World War II, the U.S. government had a 106% debt-to-GDP problem. Did they raise interest rates to 10% to fight inflation? Absolutely not.

The Fed stepped in and capped interest rates at 2.5%, while inflation ran at 6%, 8%, or even 10%.

That is called Financial Repression. The government intentionally holds interest rates below the rate of inflation, slowly eroding the purchasing power of cash and bonds to shrink the debt in real terms. It’s a hidden tax on every saver in America.

Your Survival Guide: How to Invest for What Lies Ahead

So, how do you protect yourself when the game is rigged to erode paper money?

For decades, the standard advice was the “60/40 portfolio”—put 60% of your money in stocks and 40% in government bonds, then sit back and retire. In an era of fiscal dominance, that strategy is broken. Long-term government bonds yielding less than the real cost of living are guaranteed to lose purchasing power.

The Financial Playbook My Firm Is Following for Clients

  1. Own Businesses with Real Cash Flow, Not Promises
    In a high-rate world, companies that don’t make money today are toxic. Move money away from debt-heavy, speculative tech stocks trading at nosebleed valuations. Focus on Defensive Value: Healthcare, Consumer Staples, Utilities. These are companies that sell everyday necessities, generate hard cash today, and pay reliable dividends.

  2. Overweight Energy and Master Resources
    Energy is the lifeblood of everything we do. Between geopolitical strife in the Middle East and the massive electric power demanded by new AI data centers, global energy supplies are tight. Owning oil, gas, and power infrastructure gives your portfolio an ironclad inflation hedge.

  3. Demand Clean Balance Sheets
    Avoid companies drowning in junk debt. When that 2027 refinancing wall hits corporate America, weaker businesses will see their profit margins crushed by higher interest costs. Stick with companies with little to no debt and ample cash reserves.

  4. Don’t Panic into 100% Cash
    A lot of frightened investors throw their hands in the air and move everything into cash. That’s a mistake. While cash pays a decent nominal return today, financial repression guarantees that inflation will outrun cash over time. Plus, with corporate share buybacks running hot and short-sellers heavily short, markets can stage violent rallies when you least expect it.

  5. Hold Real, Tangible Assets: Gold
    If history teaches us one undeniable lesson, it is this: whenever governments find themselves with too much debt, they always choose to debase the currency. They have done it from ancient Rome to 18th-century France to post-WWII America.

Physical gold is nobody’s liability. It cannot be printed by a central bank, and it cannot be defaulted on by a politician. In an age of financial repression, gold remains the ultimate monetary anchor.

The Bottom Line

You don’t need to fear the future, but you do need to understand the rules of the game we are playing.

The 2026–2027 debt wall is a mathematical certainty. Washington cannot borrow trillions of dollars forever without consequences, and the Federal Reserve will eventually be forced to choose between defending its currency or bailing out the Treasury.

Keep your head clear, tune out the daily market cheerleaders, avoid debt-choked companies, and anchor your wealth in tangible, cash-flowing assets.

Until next time, stay disciplined, stay safe, and always keep your eye on the Big Picture.

data.title: The Index Looks Fine. The Heat Map Does Not.
data.description:
WallStreetBets does not usually hand you a clean research note. Last night it handed everyone a giant red rectangle.

A Discussion post titled Last 4-month heat map blew up with roughly 4,000 upvotes and hundreds of comments. The picture is the familiar market map: boxes sized by company size, colored by how far prices have moved, and almost every box is blood red. Nvidia (NVDA) sits near 40% below its recent high, while memory names, chip-equipment stocks, and storage names look even worse. Google (GOOGL), Oracle (ORCL), and Caterpillar (CAT) got painted with the same brush.

The original poster put the quiet part in plain English. This has been a crash under the hood, even if the S&P 500 has not tagged a clean 10% drop yet. That line is the whole argument, and my take lines up with it. The headline index can still look like a messy correction while the engine room of this bull market is already in full drawdown. If your portfolio lives in the red boxes, the map is telling you the truth faster than the S&P number on cable.

What the map is actually showing

People argue about start dates on these charts, and they should. A fixed calendar return from July is not the same thing as a fall from each stock's own high over the last few months. When you line the big tiles up against real prices, the honest read is closer to peak-to-now pain inside a roughly four-month window of highs.

Nvidia topped near $239 in early October and recently traded near $146, about a 40% hole from that high. The semiconductor ETF that tracks the group is still roughly a third below its June peak. Intel (INTC) and ARM are about 60% off their early-summer highs, and Sandisk is on the order of two-thirds lower from its June spike. Micron (MU) and the big equipment names that feed the fabs fill in more of the damage.

Now put the polite index next to that mess. The S&P 500, through SPY, is only about 8% under its early-October high near $779. The Nasdaq-100 path is uglier, down about 15% from the same peak week, and the Dow has slipped back under 50,000. None of those index moves match the temperature of a map where the largest technology tiles look like a stop sign. Indexes are averages with weights, so a handful of survivors can keep the headline from looking like a crash while the prior leadership gets cut in half. That gap is the story.

The survivors are doing real work

Look past the loudest red boxes and you can see why the S&P still has people arguing. Apple (AAPL) has barely given back its recent high and is still solidly up on the year. Microsoft (MSFT) has been one of the adult names in the room on a multi-month calendar view even after a pullback from its own peak, and Amazon (AMZN) has been choppy rather than ruined. Those weights matter, because when the biggest household names hold up better than the speculative AI stack, the index can grind lower without ever looking like 2022 on a chart you glance at once a day.

Breadth can rot while the brand-name average keeps its dignity, which is how investors get talked into thinking they own "the market" when they really own last year's winners at this year's prices. Wall Street will call it healthy rotation. Sometimes rotation is real, and sometimes it is a polite word for the old leadership breaking while a few mega-caps still pay the rent for the index.

Why the under-the-hood crash matters

I am not calling for a cartoon collapse from here, and I am not telling you to light your account on fire. I am saying the heat map is a better dashboard than a single percentage on the S&P.

If the bull market of the last few years was sold as an artificial-intelligence buildout story, then Nvidia, memory, equipment, and the software hanging off that spend are not side shows. They are the plot. A world where those names are down 30% to 60% from their highs while commentators shrug at an 8% index drawdown is a world where risk already showed up, and it showed up first in the places that ran the hardest.

The useful part of the Reddit thread is the admission that index calm and portfolio pain can live in the same month. For anyone holding stocks through this, the practical questions are boring on purpose. How much of what you own is the red cluster on that map? How much leverage, direct or through products that sell when volatility rises, sits on top of those names? Do you still have cash if the under-the-hood crash runs longer than the cable segment about it? Forced sellers do not wait for a perfect bear-market label. They sell when the collateral math says sell.

Watch the falsifiers, not the hot takes. If credit stays orderly while chips thrash, you are often watching a leadership break and a positioning unwind. If credit cracks and the index ballast names finally join the red sea, the under-the-hood story becomes everybody's problem. If Apple-and-Microsoft-class ballast keeps holding the average together while the AI stack stabilizes on real earnings rather than hope, the map can heal from the inside without a full capitulation speech.

Bottom Line

The WallStreetBets heat map is loud because it is honest. The S&P can sit about 8% under its peak and still hide a real crash in the AI and semiconductor engine that powered the rally. Trust the red boxes you actually own more than the polite index percentage on TV, and know your leverage before the next leg decides it for you.

data.title: Circular Financing Doesn’t End With Nvidia: Amazon And Google Edition
data.description:
Jensen Huang’s sudden departure from Nvidia (NVDA) called attention to extent that the company was using its profits and credit standing to support the customers for its chips. Between direct equity stakes, loans, and loan guarantees, Nvidia was to a large extent funding the purchases of its chips. Its role in financing customers has been so large that its likely demand for its chips will fall off sharply with a Nvidia CEO less willing to engage in dubious financing arrangements.

But the Anthropic IPO is an opportunity to remind people that the circular financing in the AI industry goes beyond Nvidia. Both Amazon (AMZN) and Alphabet (GOOGL) are major holders of Anthropic stock. Amazon made an $8 billion equity investment in Anthropic in 2023 and 2024.  It bought another $5 billion this year. Alphabet put up 2022 and another $10 billion this year. Both companies have committed to buying more stock after the IPO.

This equity investment both directly and indirectly helped Anthropic pay for the computing power that Anthropic is buying from these companies’ data centers. The direct impact is straightforward. The indirect impact is that the money from these huge, well-established companies was a tremendously important vote of confidence that made other investors more willing to give their money to Anthropic. 

To be clear, there is nothing wrong with a major company investing in a promising startup that also happens to be a customer. But it is worth noting that a substantial portion of the money that Anthropic is using to buy computing power from Amazon and Alphabet is coming directly or indirectly from Amazon and Alphabet.

The other side of this story is also noteworthy. The value of the Anthropic shares held by these companies has risen enormously since they bought their stakes. This was booked as profit for these companies. In Amazon’s case, roughly half of its income for the first nine months of 2026 is the result of the appreciation of its Anthropic holdings. In Alphabet’s case, the impact of Anthropic’s appreciation was smaller, but together with its holdings of SpaceX, stock gains accounted for $77 billion, or roughly one-third of the company’s earnings over the last year.

These figures are important to keep in mind when considering reported price-to-earnings ratios. In Amazon’s case, while the reported price-to-earnings ratio is 21, measured against profits from operations it would be close to 40. In Alphabet’s case, the reported price-to-earnings ratio would be adjusted upward from roughly 15 to 20, if it is measured against operating profits. The stock prices of these companies look seriously more elevated when adjusted for these one-time stock gains.  

The moral of the story is that the financing of AI may prove to be more complicated than the technology.

data.title: Inflation Takes On A Life Of Its Own Independent Of Oil Prices
data.description:
Driving by the local gas station, motorists are taking a sigh of relief as pump prices have declined rapidly in recent weeks—-- a reflection in the hope for a US-Iranian peace agreement will put  an end  to the disruptions in the oil market. Bond investors, reacting to the prospects of future inflation, however continue to drive up yields, and central bankers talk up the need to curb inflation with higher rates for longer. The once tight correlation between oil prices, inflation and government bonds is coming apart. 

Historically, oil price shocks, such as those in the 1970s and 1980s, had an immediate effect of driving up prices across the board. At the same time, the drop in oil prices resulted in a rapid decline in the rate of inflation—-- a sharp doubled-edge sword. Today, inflation expectations  seem to be well-anchored, such that despite a drop in the oil prices, consumer inflation seems very slow to react, putting central bankers on alert towards raising rates.

Earlier in the year, the  tight correlation between oil and government borrowing costs has defined global bond markets,as the long end of the credit markets everywhere hit highs not experienced in over a decade. So, central bankers blamed the geopolitical situation for the need  to raise rates, emanating from the Iranian conflict. But that conflict is in abeyance and oil is now flowing through the Straits of Hormuz close to pre-war levels 

Starting in 2022,  the correlation between oil prices and interest rates averaged around 25%, yet interest rates climbed steadily from 1.8% to 4%, as central banks moved off the ultra-low rates that characterized the 2020s. With the advent of the Iranian conflict,  oil prices spiked from $65/bbl to $120/bb, accompanied by a surge in  the 10-year yield  from 4.2% to 5.1%. Current estimates put the oil-interest rate  correlation at 20%-25%.

But despite steep falls in global crude benchmarks in recent weeks — in part on hopes for US-Iran peace talks — yields and expectations for rate rises have remained elevated, keeping up the pressure on governments’ and households’ finances. Central banks are focusing on a raft of conditions to guide their deliberations, and the oil prices seem to play a lesser role in their minds. Inflation is no longer confined to specific commodities, but is more generally pervasive, pushing the central bankers to tighten further.

data.title: Bitcoin’s Latest Crash Has A Silver Lining
data.description:
Recently, I explained how the midterm elections could impact the future of AI.

But artificial intelligence wasn’t the only technology affected by this month’s political shakeup.

The cryptocurrency industry spent more than $170 million trying to influence the midterms, backing candidates who promised to support digital assets and establish clearer rules for the industry.

And while many of those candidates won their races, Democrats ultimately won control of both houses of Congress.

That prompted reader MK to write in and ask:

Now that the Democrats have taken over the government, do you think that the future of crypto is going to go to the bottom or at least [go] in that direction as we have seen in the past few days after the election?

The answer isn’t as simple as you might think.

The midterms certainly created more uncertainty for the crypto industry. And with prices continuing to fall, I understand why investors are worried.

But I also believe this selloff could create some excellent buying opportunities.

Crypto’s Next Chapter

For the past several years, cryptocurrency companies have been fighting for something that most other industries take for granted.

Clear rules about how they can operate.

You see, cryptocurrencies don’t fit neatly into America’s existing financial regulations. Some digital assets function like investments. Others are used to make payments, power blockchain networks or provide access to financial services.

And for years, regulators have disagreed over which government agencies should oversee them.

But last year, Congress finally started making progress.

In July 2025, lawmakers passed the GENIUS Act, creating the first federal regulatory framework for stablecoins.

As I’ve noted before, stablecoins are cryptocurrencies designed to maintain a steady value, usually by being tied to the U.S. dollar. They allow people and businesses to transfer money using blockchain networks, often much faster than traditional banking systems.

Congress also took up another major piece of legislation called the CLARITY Act.

This bill would establish clearer rules for cryptocurrency exchanges and determine which digital assets fall under the Securities and Exchange Commission and which fall under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

The House passed the bill in July 2025 with bipartisan support. But it stalled in the Senate.

And now, with Democrats preparing to take control of Congress in January, its future is even more uncertain.

Some lawmakers want stronger consumer protections and tougher restrictions on cryptocurrency businesses.

But I don’t think the Democrats are going to spend the next two years trying to shut down an industry that has become an important part of the financial system. They also have to consider the economic consequences of making America a less attractive place for cryptocurrency companies to operate.

So I believe there’s still room for compromise, even if new legislation takes longer than the industry had hoped.

Of course, investors haven’t been waiting around to find out what Congress will do. They’ve been selling.

And it’s only gotten worse since the election.

Bitcoin (BTC) briefly fell toward $62,000 last weekend, and Ethereum (ETH) has also taken a beating, falling below $2,000 and trading near $1,800.

And, frankly, I think we could see even more selling before the market finds its footing.

Part of the reason is that cryptocurrencies have become closely connected to technology stocks. When investors sell tech stocks, they often sell their cryptocurrencies too. And that can send prices falling even faster.

Investors are also worried about rising interest rates, and money has been flowing out of bitcoin investment funds. Both have added pressure to an already nervous market.

So I wouldn’t be surprised to see bitcoin fall further and trade within a relatively narrow range for a while.

But my long-term outlook hasn’t changed.

I still see bitcoin as an alternative to the dollar, especially as government debt continues to grow. And I’m particularly optimistic about Ethereum, which I believe could outperform bitcoin as the market recovers.

Meanwhile, companies are finding new ways to put cryptocurrencies to work.

For example, BitGo recently announced that its institutional clients can earn bitcoin rewards through Stacks (STX), a project that allows developers to build financial applications using bitcoin.

And they can do it without moving their bitcoin out of BitGo’s custody.

That’s a big deal because it makes it easier for large financial institutions to earn rewards on their bitcoin holdings.

And that’s exactly the kind of progress I look for when evaluating cryptocurrency investments.

I want to see projects that are actively developing their technology, signing new deals and finding ways to attract more users.

Because even when prices are falling, those are the developments that can create opportunities for investors.

Here’s My Take

I’ve been following cryptocurrency long enough to know that market selloffs can create enormous opportunities for patient investors.

Of course, not every cryptocurrency will recover. But I’ve already identified several projects that I believe have enormous long-term potential.

In fact, I’ve recommended Ethereum and Stacks to subscribers of my Next Wave Crypto Fortunes service because I believe both could play an important role in the future of finance.

[Editor’s Note: Want to know which cryptocurrencies Ian King believes could deliver big gains as the market recovers? Call 877-422-1888 to learn more about his Next Wave Crypto Fortunes service and how you can get access to his latest recommendations.]

That said, I expect more volatility for a while.

The Nasdaq could continue pulling crypto prices lower. And Washington may take longer than investors hoped to establish clearer regulations.

But crypto will keep moving forward, regardless of what happens in Congress.

And I’m convinced investors who focus on that progress could be richly rewarded in the years ahead.

data.title: Australian Dollar Remains Under Pressure As Fed And RBA Outlooks Diverge
data.description:
AUD/USD extends losses on Friday as a sell-off in global equities dampens market sentiment and weighs on risk-sensitive currencies such as the Australian Dollar (AUD), even as falling Treasury yields take some steam out of the US Dollar (USD).

At the time of writing, the pair trades around 0.6631, at levels last seen in December 2025. Meanwhile, a sharp slide in Gold prices adds to the pressure on the Aussie, given Australia’s role as a major Gold exporter.

US Treasury yields fall across the curve as investors move out of stocks and into government bonds, with the benchmark 10-year yield slipping below 5%. The US Dollar Index (DXY) eases to around 103.75 after touching a 19-month high of 103.97 on Thursday.

Nevertheless, an increasingly hawkish Federal Reserve (Fed) outlook continues to support the US Dollar, leaving AUD/USD on track for a third straight weekly decline.

Traders have all but priced in a 25-basis-point rate hike in December and are betting on another increase in January, according to the CME FedWatch Tool. Markets also expect further hikes later in 2027 as Fed officials signal that tighter policy may be needed to bring inflation back to 2%.

The Australian Dollar is also under pressure as traders increasingly see the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) nearing the end of its tightening cycle. The central bank signalled it may pause after raising the cash rate by 25 bps to 4.85% on November 3, its fifth hike this year.

The latest jobs report prompted traders to unwind bets on another RBA hike and price in around 45 bps of rate cuts by the end of 2027, according to Reuters. Australia lost 43.5K jobs in October after shedding 36.4K in September. The unemployment rate rose to 4.9% from 4.7%, reaching its highest level in five years.

data.title: Dollar Strength Dragging Down Gold But This Is Typically A Short-Term Pattern
data.description:
Dollar strength is driving gold lower. This is a typical short-term pattern. However, the inverse correlation between gold prices and dollar strength tends to break down over the longer term. 

Gold has plummeted more than 33 percent since its January high of over $5,500. Over that same period, the dollar index (DXY) rose from 96.3 to 103.2. Meanwhile, the U.S. 10-year inflation-protected real yield has climbed from 1.89 percent to 2.83 percent.

Analysts at Heraeus call the dollar “one of gold’s most consistent price drivers” over shorter time horizons. 

“Since 1990, the correlation between daily percentage changes in the gold price and DXY has been -0.31, and -0.43 this year. Put simply, dollar-up days have tended to be gold-down days. A 1 percent rise in DXY this year has typically coincided with a little more than a 2 percent fall in gold.”

However, Heraeus analysts say the DXY explains “much less” about the gold price. 

“Gold is almost ten times higher than in 1990, while DXY, which measures the strength of the dollar against other major currencies, is only around 10 percent higher.”

This makes sense when you think it through. The dollar index measures dollar strength against other fiat currencies. And while the greenback might be the cleanest dirty shirt in the laundry, it is still being constantly devalued, along with every other fiat currency. The DXY simply shows the U.S. is inflating its currency a little more slowly than other countries. It's not that the dollar is "strong." It's just stronger than the other weaklings in the room.

In other words, a falling tide drops all ships. Over the longer term, gold prices reflect this persistent inflationary pressure. That’s why many investors hold gold as a long-term inflation hedge.

Heraeus analysts noted that adjusting those gold price gains since the 90s against the DXY leaves that long-term upward trend intact, “suggesting it reflects the erosion of major fiat currencies generally, along with real gains in gold, rather than simply a weaker dollar.” 

Heraeus researchers say real yields determine whether that long-term trend can dominate.

So, what is the real interest rate, exactly?

Simply put, the real interest rate is the interest you will earn or must pay adjusted for inflation.

By factoring out inflation effects, the real interest rate reflects the “real” cost of borrowing money and the real gain in lending.

It’s a simple calculation.

The real interest rate equals the nominal rate (the numbers quoted on the news) minus CPI.

For example, consider our 10-year Treasury bond that’s yielding 5 percent. If the CPI is 2 percent, the real interest rate is only 3 percent (5-2=3).

When the CPI is high, real rates can turn negative. That means you’re losing purchasing power even though you’re earning interest. For example, let’s say our 10-year Treasury bond has a 3 percent yield, and the CPI is 5 percent. Your real interest rate is -2 percent (3-5=-2).

That might sound crazy, but real rates often went negative in the decade preceding the 2008 Financial Crisis. 

Heraeus analysts noted that before 2022, periods of high or rising 10-year real yields closely correlated with lower and falling gold prices. 

“That relationship weakened during the 2022- 2025 price rally, when central-bank buying and other drivers outweighed the rates headwind but has reasserted itself this year. The 10-year real yield has risen from around 1.7 percent in February to above 2.8 percent, close to its highest since 2008 and sharply increasing gold’s opportunity cost.” 

Here’s what some investors miss.

In a high-inflation environment, nominal interest rates can rise even as real yields fall. This occurs when inflation outpaces rising interest rates. Rising nominal yields create the impression that rates are rising even as real rates decline.

Heraeus analysts summed it up this way. 

“Inflation supports gold over the long run only when policy lets real rates fall; for now, each ‘hot print’ is a headwind.”

 Analysts say there are signs this sudden surge in dollar strength may prove short-lived. Heraeus researchers noted that speculators have swung from a $20.5 billion net short-dollar position to a $10.7 billion net long since February. It’s the largest shift from shorts to longs since 2016.

“Similar positioning extremes have often preceded dollar weakness, although the sample is small and positioning is a poor timing signal.”

Until the Fed signals an end to this tightening cycle, gold will likely face continued price pressure. At this point, most people seem to believe the Fed can hike rates at will until it reins in inflation. However, that might be easier said than done.  When inflation keeps running hot (as it has for 68 straight months), and the Fed can't raise rates because of the debt black hole and a collapsing economy, the lid will come off the gold market. You can expect the bull market to resume in earnest.

data.title: Strong Earnings Meet Rising Stock Market Volatility
data.description:
Strong earnings and economic data meet rising risk aversion

Financial markets have faced increasing pressure despite several encouraging developments, including strong corporate earnings and resilient U.S. consumer spending. Risk aversion has increased across asset classes, reflecting a more cautious tone among investors.

As of midday Thursday, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq were both down approximately 4.5% for the week. Treasury yields declined by roughly 10 basis points, while oil and industrial metals prices also fell. Corporate credit spreads widened, reflecting broader pressure across financial markets.

The contrast between positive fundamentals and weaker market performance highlights the influence of investor sentiment, even as earnings growth and consumer spending remain resilient.

Anthropic IPO draws strong investor interest

Anthropic's (ANT) highly anticipated IPO marked a significant development for the technology sector, bringing another major AI company into public markets.

The company reported revenue growth of approximately 1,200% through September 2026. Investor demand for the offering was strong, with the IPO oversubscribed and shares gaining roughly 20% during their first trading session as of midday Thursday.

Although the initial market reception was positive, the stock also experienced considerable volatility. The combination of rapid revenue growth, strong investor demand, and volatile trading highlights the continued focus surrounding AI-related companies.

Nvidia results highlight uncertainty around the AI trade

Nvidia's (NVDA) third-quarter earnings delivered a positive surprise, but the company's share price continued to face pressure.

Following the CEO's resignation, Nvidia reported strong earnings growth. Despite an initial share price rebound, the stock reversed course, declining approximately 9% for the week and 38% from its early October high, as of midday Thursday.

The reaction reflects continued investor concerns around leadership and the broader AI trade, even as the company's underlying earnings performance remains strong.

More broadly, the third-quarter earnings season has delivered impressive results. With reporting nearly complete, S&P 500 earnings growth is tracking above 30%, extending a series of positive earnings surprises over recent quarters.

The divergence between earnings growth and share price performance highlights how investor sentiment can influence market returns, even when corporate fundamentals remain strong.

Retail sales point to a resilient U.S. consumer

U.S. consumer spending continues to show resilience despite the recent increase in market volatility.

October retail sales exceeded consensus expectations, suggesting that consumers and the broader U.S. economy remain on solid footing heading into the holiday shopping season. Early indicators of holiday spending have also been encouraging, supported by a relatively healthy labor market.

The strength in consumer spending provides another positive economic signal, even as financial markets reflect growing investor caution.

Elevated risk aversion reinforces a long-term perspective

Despite encouraging earnings and consumer spending data, risk aversion has increased considerably over the past one to two weeks.

Our investment process indicates some of the highest levels of risk aversion since March 2026. Historically, periods of unusually elevated investor caution can create a more favorable environment for subsequent returns.

This supports a disciplined, long-term approach to investing through market volatility. While risk aversion has increased across equities, commodities, and credit markets, strong corporate earnings and resilient consumer spending continue to provide encouraging signals.

data.title: The Weekender: The Proverbial Sea Of Red
data.description:
The Weekender is going out a fair bit earlier than usual today, as I’m heading up to my wife’s family farm in Phibun Mangsahan, on the banks of the Mun River in northeastern Thailand, for Loy Krathong, Thailand’s traditional festival of lights and water, celebrated on the full moon of the 12th lunar month. Looking forward to some family time, a little peace away from the trading screens, and a week of hard running mileage on the rural roads. After a bruising week in the markets, I’m overdue for a proper mental reset and, more importantly, a serious physical one. But I’ll be keeping the blog active, and hopefully the markets will finally give us something worth smiling about.

Wall Street’s Sea of Red: When the Lifeboats Start Looking Overcrowded

There’s an old saying on trading desks that markets climb a staircase and descend in an elevator. Well, Wall Street appears to have misplaced the staircase, jammed the elevator button, and discovered that the emergency exits are considerably narrower than advertised. What began as an uncomfortable wobble in the artificial-intelligence trade has turned into a full-blown global de-risking exercise, with the S&P 500 tumbling 10% from its October peak, officially entering correction territory, and the Nasdaq 100 shedding another 3.5% as the technology sector’s once-invincible aura takes a decidedly expensive beating.

And this is no longer your garden-variety bout of profit-taking, where a few overextended technology names get their wings clipped before the dip-buying cavalry rides to the rescue. The selling has spread across global equities, emerging markets, high-yield credit and precious metals. Investors are piling into Treasuries, the dollar is heading for a fourth consecutive weekly gain, and the market’s favourite hiding places are becoming increasingly difficult to distinguish from its liquidation baskets.

The irony is that Wall Street entered the week hoping two major events would clear the decks. Nvidia (NVDA)’s earnings were supposed to reassure investors that the AI spending machine remained in excellent working order, while Anthropic’s (ANT) historic IPO was expected to demonstrate that capital markets still possessed an insatiable appetite for the next generation of artificial-intelligence champions.

Instead, the market bought the anticipation and sold the celebration.

Anthropic’s shares plunged 11% on their second day of trading, leaving investors who had barely finished congratulating themselves on securing an allocation wondering whether they had purchased the future or simply financed somebody else’s exit. The enthusiasm surrounding the offering had been extraordinary, with companies throughout the AI supply chain reacting to every twist in its pricing and size. Yet once the transaction was completed, the broader technology market found itself staring at the same uncomfortable questions it had been trying to ignore.

How much longer can this extraordinary AI investment cycle sustain itself? Who ultimately earns an adequate return on the enormous capital being deployed? And what happens when the cost of financing the revolution rises at precisely the moment investors begin demanding evidence of profitability?

The technology may be revolutionary, but the financing still has to obey the laws of gravity.

The AI Champagne Has Gone Flat

The problem with speculative markets is that they rarely ring a bell at the top. They simply reach a point where genuinely good news stops producing good price action, and investors gradually discover that the marginal buyer has either exhausted his ammunition or decided the next opportunity might come at a considerably cheaper price.

That appears to be the uncomfortable territory the AI complex is entering.

Anthropic’s spectacular debut was meant to be a risk-clearing event, a financial exclamation mark confirming that the AI boom still had plenty of fuel in the tank. Instead, its second-day decline has become an emblem of the market’s changing psychology. The IPO attracted enormous demand, but that enthusiasm failed to spread into the broader technology complex, where concerns about valuations, capital expenditure and the durability of the AI investment cycle are now drowning out the familiar promises of exponential growth.

The Nasdaq 100 briefly lost more than $1 trillion in combined market value during Friday’s session, with Nvidia, Broadcom (AVGO) and SpaceX (SPCX) each surrendering more than $100 billion. Those are not the sort of numbers that disappear quietly into the market’s daily statistical noise. They represent substantial destruction of equity value in companies that have become central pillars of the technology investment narrative.

And yet, even in this sea of red, interesting currents run beneath the surface. Alphabet (GOOGL) managed to buck the selling pressure, advancing nearly 2% after suffering a sharp decline the previous session. That divergence suggests investors have not abandoned every technology business indiscriminately, even if the broader market is increasingly questioning the valuations attached to the AI buildout.

There is also a fundamental distinction between enthusiasm for artificial intelligence and confidence in the financial structures supporting its development. The enormous investment required to build data centres, develop advanced models and secure semiconductor capacity depends on access to capital at a tolerable price. The prospect of tighter regulation and higher interest rates complicates that calculation considerably.

Wall Street may still believe in the AI revolution, but belief alone doesn’t service the debt.

When Credit Markets Start Smelling Smoke

Equity markets are wonderful at generating excitement, but credit markets have an unfortunate habit of asking who is going to pay the bill.

And right now, the bond market is beginning to ask some rather pointed questions.

The widening of CCC-rated credit spreads to a reported record 1,135 basis points is one of the more troubling developments beneath the headline equity selloff. These are the weakest borrowers in the corporate credit universe, companies whose financial survival can depend heavily on continued access to refinancing and a reasonably forgiving economic environment.

When spreads widen this aggressively, the message is not simply that investors have become nervous about stock valuations. It is that lenders are demanding substantially more compensation for the possibility that some borrowers may struggle to meet their obligations.

That distinction matters enormously.

US high-yield bonds have already suffered seven consecutive sessions of losses through Thursday, with broader credit stress approaching its most uncomfortable levels since late March. The most vulnerable borrowers are now facing the prospect of tighter financing conditions just as investors are becoming less willing to absorb risk.

The equity market may be debating whether AI valuations are too high, but the credit market is beginning to question whether the financing architecture supporting parts of the boom is sufficiently robust to withstand higher rates and declining risk appetite.

And that is where a technology correction threatens to become something considerably more consequential.

When the stock market catches a cold, leveraged credit can develop pneumonia.

Gold Gets Thrown Overboard With the Furniture

Perhaps the most revealing feature of this selloff is that even gold has failed to provide its customary sanctuary.

Bullion tumbled toward $3,500 an ounce on Friday, leaving it on course for a weekly decline of approximately 8%, while silver has shed nearly 15% over five sessions. Gold’s decline to its lowest level since September 2025 is particularly striking given the simultaneous deterioration in equity markets and the resurgence of demand for defensive assets.

Under normal circumstances, one might expect a significant correction in technology shares, widening credit spreads and rising geopolitical anxiety to provide considerable support for precious metals.

But markets do not always behave according to the comfortable relationships printed in investment textbooks.

Gold is also sensitive to the direction of US real interest rates, and the prospect of a more hawkish Fed raises the opportunity cost of holding an asset that pays no income. More importantly, when investors are forced to reduce leverage or replenish liquidity, assets that can be sold quickly often become sources of cash regardless of their longer-term investment merits.

The contrast with Treasuries is telling. Government bonds are attracting defensive demand while precious metals are being liquidated alongside equities and other risk assets.

That suggests this is not simply a conventional flight to safety. There is also an element of portfolio liquidation running through the market, where investors are selling what they can rather than necessarily what they want.

Bitcoin (BTC.X) slipping below $60,000 for the first time since July adds another piece to the puzzle, while emerging-market equities have extended their decline from record levels to 20%. The global retreat from risk is broadening, and the distinction between an orderly portfolio adjustment and a more disruptive deleveraging episode is becoming increasingly important.

When investors start selling the family silver to pay the margin clerk, you know the market has moved beyond an ordinary disagreement over valuations.

The 2018 Ghost Has Returned, but the Fed Put Is Missing

There is a distinctly uncomfortable echo of 2018 in the current market behaviour, and it is worth revisiting because the similarities extend well beyond a few red numbers on an equity screen.

Back then, a relatively new Fed chair, Jerome Powell, found himself navigating the late stages of a monetary tightening cycle while financial markets wrestled with the consequences of higher interest rates. Stocks initially held up before buckling under the combined weight of tighter policy, political uncertainty and deteriorating risk appetite.

Powell’s suggestion that rates remained a considerable distance from neutral rattled investors, and the S&P 500 subsequently suffered a brutal December, falling approximately 9% during the month. Cyclical sectors, including financials, energy and materials, absorbed particularly heavy punishment.

Eventually, the pressure became sufficiently intense that prominent investors began openly questioning the wisdom of continued tightening through both higher rates and balance-sheet reduction. The Fed ultimately changed course, helping establish the conditions for a market recovery in 2019.

That historical comparison is understandably attractive to investors searching for evidence that another policy rescue might be waiting around the corner.

But there is one rather inconvenient difference.

Inflation.

Core PCE inflation was running around 2% in late 2018. Today, it is above 3%, leaving the Fed with considerably less flexibility to respond to falling asset prices without risking renewed inflation pressure.

That changes the entire policy equation.

In 2018, the Fed eventually had room to retreat. In the current environment, policymakers face the uncomfortable prospect of watching financial conditions tighten while inflation remains too elevated to justify an easy monetary-policy escape route.

The possibility of further rate increases only compounds the difficulty, particularly for growth companies whose valuations depend on earnings expected well into the future and for weaker borrowers already struggling with financing costs.

This is why the old Wall Street assumption that the Fed will eventually come riding over the hill with a monetary cavalry charge may prove considerably less reliable this time around.

The famous Fed put still exists as a market concept, but with inflation above target, its strike price may be a long way below where investors would prefer to exercise it.

The 7,000 Line in the Sand

For all the macroeconomic arguments, positioning concerns and policy uncertainties, equity traders are now confronting a much simpler question: where does the selling stop?

The S&P 500 has broken below its 200-day moving average (for the third straight session), adding a technical dimension to an already uncomfortable fundamental backdrop. This widely followed trend indicator often serves as a dividing line between routine corrections within established advances and more persistent deteriorations in market momentum.

Nothing good happens when a market breaks below the 200-day!

Attention is shifting toward the 7,000 region, where key technical support could determine whether the market establishes a more durable base or extends its decline into year-end.

The problem is that technical support levels are rarely defended by good intentions alone. They require genuine buying interest, sufficient liquidity and a willingness among investors to absorb additional risk.

At present, those ingredients appear to be in short supply.

A more aggressive capitulatory selloff could eventually help reset positioning and sentiment, creating the conditions for a healthier recovery. Markets have a long history of exhausting sellers before finding their footing, and there is nothing particularly unusual about corrections becoming more violent near their final stages.

But capitulation is a process, not a date on the calendar, and calling the bottom while credit spreads are widening and the Fed remains hawkish can be an expensive exercise in wishful thinking.

Geopolitical uncertainty adds another complication. Without a meaningful improvement in the Iran situation, elevated inflation and tighter financial conditions remain significant obstacles to any sustained recovery in risk appetite.

The coming sessions will therefore test more than the S&P 500’s ability to defend a particular technical level. They will test whether investors have reduced enough leverage, whether the AI complex can stabilize and whether the credit market can absorb the tightening in financial conditions without transmitting more serious stress into the broader economy.

A Market Running Out of Lifeboats

The most important development this week may not be that the S&P 500 has entered correction territory. Markets have survived plenty of 10% declines, and some of the most profitable advances in history have emerged from precisely these moments of discomfort.

What matters is the increasingly synchronized selling.

Technology shares are being repriced, emerging-market equities are falling into bear-market territory, speculative credit is under pressure, and gold is being liquidated despite the growing demand for safety elsewhere.

Meanwhile, the dollar continues to attract defensive flows, Treasuries are finding buyers, and investors are being forced to reconsider whether the monetary-policy environment that supported years of aggressive risk-taking is still reliable.

There is a meaningful difference between a market correcting excessive enthusiasm and a market beginning to discover that the liquidity supporting that enthusiasm was never quite as deep as everyone assumed.

The first is a valuation adjustment. The second can become a funding problem.

And with inflation still limiting the Fed’s freedom to intervene, the distinction could prove crucial.

For now, Wall Street finds itself staring at the proverbial sea of red, hoping the selling eventually burns itself out before the financial plumbing starts springing leaks.

The AI party may have supplied the champagne, but the Fed is controlling the bar tab, and the credit market is beginning to wonder who is going to settle the bill.
